(AA photo)
President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan has noted that Egypt could join the new joint defense pact alongside Türkiye, Saudi Arabia and Pakistan, signaling that the nascent alliance is open to expanding its reach.
“This agreement has sent an important message to the world,” Erdoğan told Al Jazeera in an interview aired Aug. 16. He said Egypt’s participation was among the options for expanding the agreement in the future.
The deal, known as the Mecca Pact, was signed in the holy city last week by Erdoğan, Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman and Pakistani Prime Minister Shahbaz Sharif.
Under the agreement, an armed attack against any one of the three countries would be treated as an attack against all three, establishing a collective-deterrence provision that analysts have compared with NATO’s Article 5. Officials have cautioned, however, against viewing the pact as a NATO equivalent or as being directed against any particular country.
Erdoğan’s comments came as he discussed a range of regional issues, including tensions surrounding the Strait of Hormuz and conflicts in Syria, Gaza and Lebanon.
He said reopening the Strait of Hormuz was a priority for Ankara, arguing that its continued closure served no one’s interests. Erdoğan also credited Qatar with playing an important role in mediation efforts aimed at ending fighting in the region.
“Türkiye cannot leave Gaza alone,” Erdoğan said, pledging that Ankara would do whatever was necessary to support the Palestinian territory.
He said Hamas was fulfilling its commitments in good faith while Israel continued its military campaign in Gaza.
On Syria, Erdoğan said Turkiye would do everything in its power to support stability and reiterated plans to visit the country. He also said Syria’s Kurds would have “a share of peace and stability,” adding that Türkiye would continue strengthening ties with Kurdish communities and safeguarding their rights across the region.
Erdoğan also voiced concern over continued Israeli attacks in Lebanon. He said he had raised the need to end the war in Lebanon with U.S. President Donald Trump during his recent visit to Türkiye.
The interview also touched on Türkiye’s efforts to return to the U.S.-led F-35 fighter jet program.
Türkiye was removed from the multinational program in 2019 after acquiring Russia’s S-400 air defense system, which Washington said could compromise the aircraft’s technology.
Trump said during the NATO summit in Ankara last month that his administration would lift sanctions imposed on Türkiye over the S-400 purchase. He also said a Turkish return to the F-35 program was “something certainly we’d consider.” Any potential sale still faces opposition in Congress.
Meanwhile, Erdoğan marked the 25th anniversary of his ruling Justice and Development Party (AKP) at a rally in Ankara on Aug. 14, saying he intended to remain active in politics for years to come.
“As Tayyip Erdoğan, I have left behind 50 years in politics. If God grants me life and health, I will continue to serve Türkiye for many more years,” he said.
“We are just getting started,” he added, saying the party’s movement would carry Türkiye, “God willing, first to 2053 and then to 2071.”
Founded on Aug. 14, 2001, the AKP won 34.3 percent of the vote in its first national election in November 2002, forming a single-party government.
Erdoğan was elected president for a third term in May 2023. Under AKP leadership, Türkiye transitioned from a parliamentary system to an executive presidential model in 2018, a change opposition parties have criticized.

Timeline: The one-week siege of Qusra by Israeli settlers in the West Bank
Israeli settlers encircle Palestinian homes and cut off supplies, leading to a declaration of a military zone.
Sunday marks one week since Israeli settlers began their siege of Qusra, a Palestinian village south of Nablus in the occupied West Bank.
Since August 9, dozens of Israeli settlers have surrounded three Palestinian homes in the Ras al-Ain area on the edge of the village, cutting off water and electricity as food and other supplies run low. About 15 Palestinians from the Abu Rida and Hassan families live in these homes, among them two children under the age of seven and one belonging to a dual US citizen. Residents said settlers from nearby outposts have been trying to take the properties for months.
On Thursday, the Israeli military ordered the residents of two of the houses to leave and forced them all into the third. That same day, US Ambassador to Israel Mike Huckabee, a staunch supporter of Jewish settlements in the West Bank, described the settlers besieging the homes as “Israeli terrorists“. The Office of the United Nations High Commissioner for Human Rights and the Palestinian Ministry of Foreign Affairs condemned the siege, calling it criminal and inhumane.
Over the course of the week, the Israeli army declared the area a closed military zone and blocked Israeli and foreign activists from reaching the besieged families. Reporting from Qusra on Sunday, Al Jazeera’s Nour Odeh said the UN was able to bring in some aid that morning after coordinating with the Israeli military.
Where is Qusra?
Qusra sits in Area B, which makes up about 21 percent of the West Bank. It is where the Palestinian Authority runs civil affairs, such as education, healthcare and the economy, but Israel retains full security control and its forces can enter at will.
Odeh said the sequence in Qusra is following a pattern repeated across the West Bank: The Israeli army deploys to an area, takes over Palestinian homes and dispossesses residents of their properties while settlers face no arrests.
Average of six settler attacks each day
According to the UN Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs, from January 2025 to June 2025, there were at least 3,033 settler attacks in the occupied West Bank – an average of six per day.
Settlements built illegally on Palestinian land
Last month, a similar siege in the neighbouring village of Jalud displaced Palestinian families from their land, which settlers then took over. Qusra itself has faced repeated attacks, including the burning of a newly built mosque last month.
Since October 7, 2023, when Israel’s genocidal war in Gaza began, settler attacks and land grabs have intensified in the West Bank under Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s right-wing government, which has backed a rapid expansion of settlements.
About 700,000 Israelis live in settlements, which are illegal under international law. About three million Palestinians also live in the West Bank. Israel has occupied the region since 1967.

Cambridge University defends its mental health support for Jason Arday
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-16
13:16:38 UTC
22:16:38 KST

The University of Cambridge has defended its mental health support for the academic Jason Arday.
The university said it had continued to provide Arday with extensive mental health support and security measures, including installing panic alarms and screening racist emails and post, after he resigned from his post as professor of sociology of education this month.
He quit after widespread press coverage of accusations of plagiarism and inconsistencies in statements about his career and achievements.
A University of Cambridge spokesperson said: “Our support continued in the face of intense public and media scrutiny and after his resignation. Our thoughts and deepest condolences are with Jason’s family and loved ones at this extremely difficult time.”
Arday, 41, was pronounced dead after emergency services were called to his home in Battersea, south London, on Friday.
When he was appointed professor of sociology of education at Cambridge at the age of 37 in 2023, he was the university’s youngest ever black professor.
A vigil in Arday’s memory organised by the campaign group Stand Up to Racism will be held on the steps of the National Gallery in Trafalgar Square, central London, at 6pm on Monday. The group’s co-convener Weyman Bennett said in a statement that Arday’s death was the “result of a racist witch-hunt”.
He added: “For more than a week, the rightwing press, politicians and the far right have hounded Jason with the most vicious racism. They are spreading the far-right lie that black people are only appointed because of the colour of our skin, rather than our ability.”
Arday was initially accused of plagiarising another academic’s work for his PhD thesis. He denied the accusations, and an investigation by Liverpool John Moores University this year upheld its decision to award him a PhD.
When allegations surfaced in the UK media in July, Cambridge said it had investigated the claims and found no wrongdoing, describing Arday as the victim of a “vile smear campaign to undermine his credibility”.
This month, the university announced it would open a fresh investigation after it said it received “new information” about Arday’s qualifications and career.
Other elements of Arday’s life story were increasingly questioned, including claims of prodigious money-raising for charity and feats of long-distance running. He was also challenged about whether he was nonverbal until the age of 11, as well as being illiterate until 18.
It is understood Cambridge has paused the investigation while Arday’s family are grieving, and will consider whether to reopen it in due course.
Academics and politicians have cast doubt on whether Cambridge took Arday’s vulnerability seriously when he was appointed to the senior public-facing role in 2023. At the time, the university had been facing criticism for its lack of diversity in senior roles.
Prof Simon Baron-Cohen, Arday’s friend and former colleague, told Times Radio he thought the university should proceed with the investigation. “We should see what we learn from it. This is the whole purpose of investigations,” he said.
He also questioned whether the media had failed in its duty of care towards Arday, as a vulnerable person with disabilities. He said Arday faced racist abuse and was used as a “lightning rod for a culture war on [diversity, equity and inclusion]”.
Lord Simon Woolley, the principal of Homerton College, Cambridge, and Arday’s former mentor, has called for an investigation into the “vicious media onslaught”.
In a statement on Saturday, Prof Deborah Prentice, the vice-chancellor of Cambridge University, said her “thoughts and deepest condolences” were with Arday’s family, as well as with colleagues and students in the faculty of education and at Jesus College where he was a fellow.
“Supporting our community through this tragedy is the single most important priority for me and my leadership team right now. We will be reaching out to many of you directly, and we are committed to ensuring that no one feels they must face this alone,” she said.
A fundraiser launched by the Windrush campaigner Patrick Vernon on Saturday afternoon has raised more than £65,000 to contribute towards funeral and memorial costs and support for Arday’s family.
On the crowdfunder’s webpage, Vernon said: “I was one of the people who publicly supported Jason during the recent controversy because I was deeply concerned about the nature and intensity of the attacks directed towards him. I was also subject to media scrutiny for signing the letter of support and challenged in supporting Jason.”
Andy Burnham, the prime minister, described Arday’s death as a “tragedy on so many levels” and urged a “moment of reflection”.
In a statement issued via Simon & Schuster, which published Arday’s memoir, Great and Unfortunate Things, in the US this week, Arday’s family said they were “in shock to have lost this amazing father, partner, brother, uncle and son”.
They added: “Jason was subjected to a campaign of sustained abuse for more than three years since he accepted the role of professor at Cambridge University by those who would leave no stone unturned in their quest to undermine him. The campaign of misinformation was too much for Jason, who was a gentle man and who always wanted to see the best in everyone.”

Authorities in several Russian regions and occupied Crimea have begun implementing restrictions on fuel sales and prices to combat shortages, The Moscow Times reported.
The Orenburg region has introduced strict limits on gasoline and diesel sales. The measures follow a Ukrainian drone attack that disabled the Orsknefteorgsintez refinery, which has an annual capacity of 5.7 million tons.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
Under the new rules, gas stations in the region will only sell a maximum of 30 liters of AI-92 and AI-95 gasoline per vehicle. Diesel purchases are capped at 60 liters within settlements and 200 liters on highways, while filling portable canisters is now prohibited.
Prior to this, the Federal Antimonopoly Service (FAS) had investigated propane prices in the region, which had increased by 1.5 times over two months to 42-45 rubles ($0,50-0,54) per liter.
On Aug. 14, authorities in the Novosibirsk region announced an agreement with oil traders and gas station networks to cap the retail markup on fuel at a maximum of 15% above the wholesale price provided by Gazprom Neft.
Regional officials described this as the first agreement of its kind in Russia. It is set to remain in effect until Nov. 15, with the possibility of an extension.
Sergei Latskikh, president of the Siberia-GSM Association of Independent Oil Traders, stated that the practice is intended to stabilize regional markets and prevent speculative pricing.
On-the-Lam Polish Politician Surfaces in Renegade, Pro-Moscow Moldova Territory
In temporarily occupied Crimea, the situation has been particularly volatile. When open fuel sales briefly resumed on Aug. 4, prices surged, reaching between 195 and 270 rubles (approximatelybetween $2.30 and $3.21) per liter for AI-92 and AI-95 gasoline.
In response, occupation authorities announced a strict price ceiling of 100 rubles ($120) per liter for AI-92 and indicated that limits for other fuel grades would be established by mid-August. Subsequently, the peninsula returned to a rationing system utilizing QR codes for fuel purchases.
Collapse of Crimean tourism
The fuel crisis, combined with electricity outages caused by Ukrainian drone strikes on electrical substations, has mpacted Crimea’s tourism industry. Hotel bookings have fallen more than 70% compared to July of the previous year.
The Russian government has pledged over 4.3 billion rubles ($54 million) in one-time payments to support tourism workers, offering an amount equivalent to three months of the minimum wage.
Despite the strikes, some tourists from nearby Russian regions continue to visit. Some travelers arriving by road from the Krasnodar region reported bringing jerry cans filled with petrol to ensure they had fuel for the return journey.
Reported plans to replace Aksyonov
The worsening infrastructure and supply issues have led to reports of planned leadership changes in occupied Crimea.
In late July, the Ukrainian partisan movement Atesh, citing agents within the occupation administration, reported that the Kremlin plans to remove Sergei Aksyonov, the Russian-installed head of Crimea, following elections scheduled for September.
According to Atesh, Moscow intends to blame Aksyonov for the humanitarian and infrastructure problems, including the disruptions to electricity, water, and fuel supplies, to reduce social tensions and deflect blame from the central government.
The partisan group noted that Alexei Dmitriev, the Russian-appointed interior minister in Crimea, is considered a leading candidate to replace Aksyonov, signaling a potential shift toward tighter control by Russian security services.

'Time to come home': Seven families from New York's Persian Jewish community make aliyah together
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-16
13:13:19 UTC
22:13:19 KST

This article was written in collaboration with Nefesh B'Nefesh
Seven families from the Persian Jewish community of Great Neck, New York, arrived at Tel Aviv's Ben-Gurion Airport last Tuesday, exhausted from their journey but excited for their lives as new immigrants to Israel.
“We’re running on fumes, but exhilarated,” Jordan, one of the new olim (immigrants) and a father of six girls, told The Jerusalem Post at the airport, adding that there were “too many emotions to process properly” but that he felt as though he was “flying.”
The families, which included some 26 children, made aliyah (immigration to Israel) with the help of Nefesh B’Nefesh, the non-profit organization that facilitates immigration to Israel from the United States and Canada, in partnership with Israel’s Ministry of Aliyah and Integration, the Jewish Agency for Israel, Keren Kayemeth LeIsrael, and Jewish National Fund-USA.
“The decision of these seven families to make aliyah together and choose Israel as their home is both visionary and deeply meaningful,” said Naftali Derovan, Head of the Aliyah Guidance Division at Nefesh B’Nefesh. “They remind us that while Aliyah is often a deeply personal decision, it can also be a communal one. In this case, these families are bringing the strength and spirit of their close-knit community with them to Israel. We are excited to continue providing them with the professional support and resources they need to integrate successfully, build their lives here, and truly feel at home in Israel.”
After arriving, the new olim received their official Israeli ID cards before eventually being shuttled to their new homes in the central city of Ra'anana.
Ra'anana mayor says city is proud to absorb new immigrants
“We warmly welcome the new families joining our community and are deeply moved by this inspiring step, which embodies Zionism and faith,” said the Mayor of Ra’anana, Chaim Broyde. “Ra’anana is proud to be one of Israel’s leading cities in the absorption of new immigrants, serving as a home to olim from dozens of countries and bringing together diverse communities.”
“We embrace the new olim and are committed to providing them and their children with the support they need to integrate, thrive, and feel at home in Ra’anana,” he added. “I wish the families a smooth transition into their new lives, and assure them that we will be there to support them every step of the way.”
Before leaving the airport, though, as they passed through customs and entered the Terminal 3 arrivals hall, the new olim were greeted by a jubilant crowd of mostly teenagers who sang and cheered as they welcomed them to Israel.
Among those were a group of girls who had done Sherut Leumi (national service) in Great Neck, alongside the very members of the Persian community who made aliyah.
Amid the scramble to make sure everything was in order after entering the arrivals hall, the new olim told the Post that the American-Persian Jewish community was “hearing the call to come back” to Israel.
“We're expecting many more in the next year, and b’ezrat Hashem (with God's help), this is going to be something for many years to come. You're going to see a lot of the Persian communities coming back,” Jordan said.
Adam, another of the olim and a father of five, said that the community members had gotten together and “decided it’s time to come home.”
“Each family wanted to do it for a long time, and suddenly we came together and said, ‘It's so hard to come alone. You feel lonely. You feel like you miss people. Why not do it together?’ Seven families are here together today, back home. It's a dream come true.”
Adam added that he also expected many more from the Persian Jewish community to make aliyah from the US, saying that the movement to come to Israel was “on fire.”
Persian-Jewish aliyah group hopes to entice other community members
Jen, another member of the group, said that they hoped that, because they came as a group, it would help entice other community members and make their moves easier.
That community back in New York, she said, was elated for those who had made the move to Israel.
“Over the course of the past few weeks, every Shabbos we were being celebrated,” she said. “They're honoring us in shul (synagogue), and they had a whole group of people who came and met us by the coach bus yesterday and sent us off.”
Talia, another woman in the group and a mother of three, said the decision to move to Israel was made in part because, despite “an amazing life in New York,” they are “thinking about our kids and the future of Jewish life.”
“We believe that the future of ‘Am Yisrael’ (the Jewish people) is in Israel, and we have this opportunity to do it all together,” she said.

Knesset asks High Court to unfreeze budget transfers approved during election recess
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-16
13:13:11 UTC
22:13:11 KST

The Knesset asked the High Court of Justice on Sunday to allow five frozen budget transfers to proceed, arguing that Speaker Amir Ohana acted within his authority when he approved a Finance Committee meeting during the election recess.
The court is due to hear the petition on Tuesday, with hundreds of millions of shekels in disputed allocations still on hold. The case could also determine how far the Knesset speaker may go in authorizing parliamentary business after the usual coalition-opposition mechanism for approving recess meetings has rejected it.
Justice Alex Stein temporarily halted nearly all the transfers on August 5, citing apparent problems with the way the committee had been convened. He allowed one allocation concerning civilian emergency expenses to proceed and referred the case to a three-justice panel.
The temporary order did not determine whether the meeting or the transfers were unlawful. It will remain in place unless the court lifts or changes it.
The Hiddush religious-freedom organization and Democrats MK Naama Lazimi filed the petition. They argue that the August 4 meeting breached special restrictions governing the Knesset during the election recess and allowed the coalition to approve politically sensitive spending less than three months before the October 27 election.
The Knesset’s central response is that its rules provide two separate ways to convene committees during a recess.
Under the ordinary route, meetings require approval from a Coordination Committee representing both the coalition and opposition. A separate provision allows the speaker to authorize additional meetings in “special cases” at the request of the government, the committee chairman, or one-third of its members.
Knesset: House Committee decision cannot cancel speaker's authority
The Knesset argued that the second route remains available even when the Coordination Committee has refused approval. It said a decision adopted by the House Committee for the election recess could not cancel authority expressly granted to the speaker.
The dispute began after the Knesset entered its election recess on July 18. The recess is due to continue until the next Knesset is sworn in following the October election.
The House Committee had approved rules allowing the Finance Committee to hold one meeting concerning budget transfers during the first two weeks of the recess. Meetings generally required four days’ notice, although the speaker could shorten that period in urgent and exceptional circumstances.
The Finance Committee held the permitted meeting on July 29. According to the Knesset’s response, 33 budget requests had been published before the meeting. The committee considered 23 by the time the sitting ended at 7:30 p.m. and approved 22.
Finance Committee chairman MK Hanoch Milwidsky subsequently sought another meeting to consider 13 requests that had not been addressed, along with three requests for reconsideration.
Government ministries were asked to explain which transfers were urgent. The government ultimately prioritized six, and the Knesset’s legal advisers concluded that those six could be discussed because of their stated importance and urgency.
The Coordination Committee did not approve another meeting after opposition coordinator MK Merav Ben-Ari objected. Milwidsky then asked Ohana to authorize it through the separate “special cases” provision.
Ohana accepted the legal advisers’ position that the six transfers justified another meeting. He also shortened the required notice period from four days to three, despite the Knesset legal adviser’s position that no reason had been given for departing from the four-day rule.
All requests approved by Finance Committee despite objections
The Finance Committee convened on August 4 and approved all six requests. Opposition lawmakers argued at the meeting that it had been unlawfully called and that some of the spending was inconsistent with the restraint expected during an election campaign.
The allocations covered a broad range of spending and internal budget changes. The Knesset said the ministries had identified needs including defense expenditure, preparations for the school year, salaries, payments to suppliers, summer education programs, and preventing the shutdown of the rabbinical courts’ computer systems.
The requests also included coalition funds for religious and haredi education and programs connected to the National Missions Ministry. One Education Ministry request included approximately NIS 268 million in coalition allocations. Other requests included NIS 125 million for the National Missions Ministry and about NIS 78 million for the Religious Services Ministry.
The Knesset said all six requests had completed the government approval process, including review by government legal advisers, before reaching the committee. It argued that claims concerning improper government spending should be directed principally at the government, rather than used to invalidate the parliamentary meeting.
It also said approval by the Finance Committee only makes funding available and does not independently authorize a government program or permit unlawful expenditure.
The Knesset further argued that the present government is not formally a caretaker government because it has not resigned, lost a no-confidence vote, or been replaced following an election. Restrictions developed by the court for caretaker governments therefore cannot simply be applied to the Knesset’s internal work, it said.
Ohana’s use of the provision was not unprecedented, according to the response. The Knesset said the speaker authorized three Finance Committee meetings during the 2022 election recess after the Coordination Committee declined to approve them. Some of those meetings also concerned coalition funds.
The Knesset concluded that courts intervene only rarely in the internal management of parliamentary proceedings and that no defect in this case justified overturning the committee’s decisions.
It asked the court to dismiss the petition and lift the order. The petitioners will argue on Tuesday that the August meeting bypassed safeguards intended to prevent the governing coalition from using public funds without sufficient opposition oversight during an election campaign.

UK Dept Ed. reviewing Muslim schools run by Al-Khair Foundation following reports of Hamas ties
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-16
13:13:05 UTC
22:13:05 KST

The UK's Department of Education (DfE) is assessing information regarding four Muslim independent schools after the Charity Commission opened a statutory inquiry into the Al-Khair Foundation, the organization that runs the schools.
As reported by the The Jerusalem Post on August 9, the UK Charity Commission is investigating the prominent Muslim-registered charity Al-Khair Foundation following reports of alleged Hamas connections.
Al-Khair was set up to advance religion, promote education, support social welfare, build religious harmony, and offer relief to victims of disasters.
However, the Commission said it received a complaint alleging the charity and its partners had connections to Hamas and had also funded Hamas.
The regulator immediately started examining the serious concerns raised and gathered more information to inform its assessment. The Commission has now escalated its engagement to a statutory inquiry.
Al-Khair employee charged with conspiring to provide material support to Hamas
This follows the arrest of Mohammad Yousef Hasna, an individual employed by Al-Khair Foundation, in the UK last week. Hasna was extradited to the US and charged with conspiring to provide material support to Hamas.
This prompted UK Lawyers for Israel (UKFLI) to send a report to the DfE's Counter-Extremism Division on 10 July 2026, detailing Al-Khair’s links to the Hamas terrorist group and raising concerns about safeguarding, extremism, and compliance with the Prevent duty at schools operated by the charity.
The Post viewed correspondence between UKFLI and the DfE regarding the Al Khair Foundation. DfE said it is "continuing to work with other government departments and agencies to assess all the information that has been provided to us and determine next steps"
The four schools run by Al Khair Foundation are Al-Khair Preparatory School in Croydon; Al-Khair Preparatory School in Oldbury, Birmingham; and Al-Khair Secondary Schools for Boys and Girls in Croydon. Over 550 children attend the four schools. The annual school fees are £5468 for the Croydon schools and £3600 for the Birmingham school.
UKLFI's letter to the DfE warned that the schools could be exposed to safeguarding and Prevent-related risks arising from Al-Khair’s employment of individuals allegedly linked to proscribed terrorist organizations. UKLFI's investigation found that at least two people employed by Al-Khair Foundation had been identified as Hamas operatives, while another employee had significant links with Hamas figures.
UK schools required to assess risk of pupils being drawn into extremism
Schools are subject to the statutory Prevent duty, requiring them to assess the risk of pupils being drawn into terrorism, challenge extremist narratives and manage potentially harmful external influences. UKLFI said the evidence it had gathered justified examination of whether those safeguards were operating effectively at the Al-Khair schools.
A UKLFI spokesperson said, "The allegations concerning Al-Khair Foundation are extremely serious in themselves, but they become still more concerning when an organization facing such allegations is also responsible for the education and safeguarding of children."
"UKLFI alerted the Department to these concerns because schools must have robust procedures to protect pupils from extremist influence and from being drawn into support for terrorism. We hope the Department will now examine carefully the governance of all four schools, their relationships with the Foundation and its personnel, and whether their safeguarding and Prevent obligations have been properly discharged.
"The Charity Commission's statutory inquiry and the separate criminal allegations now being pursued by the US authorities underline why these concerns required urgent investigation."

Hamas’s popularity is falling, but Khalil al-Hayya remains more popular than PA’s Abbas - poll
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-16
13:12:37 UTC
22:12:37 KST

Though Hamas’s popularity has declined among Palestinians in the West Bank and Gaza, Hamas leader Khalil al-Hayya still commands more support than PA President Mahmoud Abbas, according to a new poll published by the Ramallah-based Palestinian Center for Policy and Survey Research on Wednesday.
The survey was conducted among 1,270 Palestinians between August 5 and 8, with 830 respondents in the West Bank and 440 in the Gaza Strip. Researchers conducted assisted face-to-face interviews using tablets or mobile phones, with the data automatically transmitted to the research center’s server to prevent interception or manipulation. The poll had a margin of error of 3.5%.
The most popular candidate for Palestinian leadership was Fatah figure Marwan Barghouti, who is currently imprisoned in Israel and played a key role in the Second Intifada, with 54% of likely voters saying they would vote for him in a hypothetical presidential election.
Al-Hayya would receive just over a quarter of the votes, 26%, and the current Palestinian Authority president would receive only 14%, according to the poll. Notably, only 10 months ago, 36% of respondents said they would support senior Hamas figure Khaled Meshaal, showing a drop in support by 10%.
Satisfaction with Abbas’s performance as president stands at just 20%, down slightly from 23% 10 months ago, while 76% of Palestinians expressed dissatisfaction, according to the poll. Satisfaction was higher in Gaza, at 26%, than in the West Bank, where just 16% approved of his performance.
The large majority, 82% in the West Bank and 74% in the Strip, want to see Abbas’s resignation.
Likely connected to Abbas’s lack of popularity, 83% of respondents said that they believed that there is corruption in PA institutions and 65% said they view the authority as a burden for Palestinians.
Election turnout could be high if factions from the 2006 vote participate in today's elections
Despite more than half expressing support for Barghouti, 40% said they would not participate in the presidential elections. However, if legislative elections were held in which all electoral lists or factions that participated in the 2006 elections competed, turnout would be 66%.
Fatah would receive 32% of the votes in the legislative elections, according to the poll, followed by Hamas at a close 29%. However, among Gazan respondents alone, Hamas would receive 34%, Fatah 30%, and the combined third parties 27%.
Though more than a quarter of respondents maintained their position in favor of Hamas, the poll showed a significant decline in support for the terrorist group. Just 10 months ago, 44% of respondents overall said they would vote for Hamas, and support in Gaza specifically stood at 49%.
When asked which political party or political orientation they supported, 24% said they preferred Fatah, and 24% answered that they preferred Hamas; 14% chose third parties, and 38% said they supported none of them or did not know.
Continuing to demonstrate a trend in declining support for Hamas, ten months ago, 35% said they supported Hamas, including 41% in Gaza, but the figure now stands at only 18% in the West Bank and 33% in Gaza.
Though the survey did not seek to determine if, when, or why respondents’ views of Hamas had changed, it found that only 20% believed Hamas emerged victorious from the war against Israel. A majority, 60%, said neither side won, while 15% said Israel emerged victorious. In the Gaza Strip, 20% said Hamas won, while an identical 20% said Israel emerged victorious.
The proportion of respondents who believed Hamas had won the war nearly halved from 39% in October 2025. The decline was particularly pronounced in the West Bank, where just 21% now believe Hamas emerged victorious, down from 48% 10 months ago.
Not as popular as it once was, 72% of respondents were still against Hamas disarming before a complete Israeli withdrawal from the Gaza Strip.
Only 20% of respondents felt Hamas should disarm first. Palestinians living in the Gaza were slightly more in favor of Hamas disarming first, with 62% opposed, compared to the West Bank, where 79% insisted Israeli presence must first be removed.
Respondents believe war would resume if Hamas disarmed, Israel would not withdraw from Gaza
An overwhelming majority, 72%, said they believed that if Hamas were to disarm, the war in Gaza would resume and Israel would not fully withdraw from the Strip. Only 22% believed that Hamas’s disarmement would not be the cause of a continued war.
One in five respondents said they believed a full-scale war would resume, while only 30% believed Gaza would move toward a period of peace and stability. Another 41% said they expected the current situation, marked by occasional Israeli strikes, to continue.
Support for a two-state solution has remained largely unchanged over the past 10 months, with 44% of respondents in favor, down one percentage point from October, while 50% opposed the proposal, according to the poll.
Some 58% said that the two-state solution is no longer practical because of settlement expansion, while 36% answered that they believe that it remains practical. Similarly, 64% say that the chances of establishing an independent Palestinian state alongside Israel within the next five years are low or nonexistent, while 32% say that the chances are medium or high. With the two-state solution being a divisive issue among Palestinians, 36% said they supported the alternative of returning to confrontations and armed intifada, and 33% said they supported a single Palestinian state.
More than half (53%) also said they believed that even if Hamas gave up its weapons, it would remain an “armed resistance movement,” as well as a political movement, while only 36% believed it would focus solely on politics.
Trust in the US-backed alternative to Hamas, the Board of Peace, was low, but it was considered a viable political option, the survey found.
If the Palestinian elections scheduled for November are held as planned and a new government is formed, 32% (43% in Gaza and 24% in the West Bank) would prefer that NCAG maintain responsibility for the Strip over the elected government.
Only 28% (34% in Gaza and 24% in the West Bank) would prefer a newly elected government to assume responsibility for the administration of Gaza, while 34% do not prefer either option.
Asked their opinion of external actors, the Iran-aligned Houthi terror group was highly popular among respondents in both Gaza and the West Bank. The majority, 61% (63% in the West Bank and 58% in Gaza), said they were satisfied with the Houthis.
Qatar (51%), Hezbollah (50%) and Iran (50%) were also popular among Palestinian respondents, though satisfaction with Iran has grown over the past 10 months and Doha’s popularity has slightly declined since the last survey.
When asked whether they were with or against Iran during the recent war between the United States and Iran, which resulted in the closure of the Strait of Hormuz and retaliatory attacks against US bases in the region, 45% of respondents said that they were with Iran, 12% answered that they were against Iran, and 40% said that they were neither with Iran nor with the United States.

How a Chinese UAV has become a Ukrainian long-range weapon
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-16
16:11:00 EEST
22:11:00 KST

How a Chinese UAV has become a Ukrainian long-range weapon: the story of the mysterious MICH 2000 drone
In early August, Ukrainian forces hit the cargo ship Nadezhda near the Russian Black Sea port of Novorossiysk.
Footage of the strike soon circulated across social media and Telegram channels. Yet the drone at the centre of it looked nothing like a Liutyi or an FP-1, two systems widely used by the Ukrainian military in long-range strikes on Russia. Instead, it bore a striking resemblance to the Iranian-designed Shahed, leaving analysts scratching their heads over what exactly they were looking at.
This was not the first time Shahed-like drones had been used in attacks on targets inside Russia. Among the possible candidates were the Egyptian-made Jabbar-150, Türkiye's Troy T20 Block 20 and China's ZTK-150.
The drone in question is, in fact, the Ukrainian MICH-2000. But those who thought footage of the strikes showed Chinese-made ZTK-150s were not entirely wrong either.
This drone's story began thousands of kilometres from the front line – not in a Ukrainian garage or design office, but at a factory in China. In late 2023, Ukrainian UAV developers travelled there to acquire ready-made civilian UAVs for military use. Nobody at the time could have known that the mission would lay the groundwork for a Ukrainian long-range drone – the kind of system the military, engineers and politicians in Ukraine commonly call a "deep-strike" UAV.
Today, the MICH is no longer simply a Chinese-made drone, but a system operated exclusively by the Security Service of Ukraine's Special Operations Centre Alpha. Capable of flying up to 2,000 km and carrying as much as 60 kg of explosives, it is building an ever-longer record of targets struck inside Russia.
Ukrainska Pravda has visited the factory producing the MICH-2000 to tell, for the first time, the story of how a trip in search of Chinese-made drones kick-started the production of a Ukrainian long-range drone for the Alpha.
All material presented in this story has been cleared for publication by the manufacturer and the Security Service of Ukraine.
A MICH 2000 striking its target. Video: Exilenova+, a Ukrainian Telegram channel
A "little plane" from China
The use of Chinese-made drones as long-range weapons dates back to 2022. Ukraine was then only taking its first steps towards developing systems of its own, such as the Liutyi and FP-1. But the need to reach targets deep behind enemy lines was already there. Until its own drones were ready, the simplest answer was to buy off-the-shelf aircraft from China.
The Ukrainian military adapted civilian Mugin-5 PRO drones for military use, fitted them with explosives and launched them on targets far behind Russian lines. At around US$15,000 apiece, the aircraft could carry up to 25 kg of explosives to targets as far as 500 km away.
The use of unidentified Chinese-made drones to strike targets inside Russia did not remain under the radar for long. Media reports began to draw attention to them, and China eventually responded. In the summer of 2023, the Communist Party imposed restrictions on the direct export of civilian drones. With the aircraft suddenly harder to obtain, Ukrainian buyers had to find ways around the new barriers.
Towards the end of 2023, a team of Ukrainian UAV engineers received an assignment from the military: travel to China, buy what they referred to simply as "little planes" from local manufacturers, and bring them back to Ukraine.
When the team arrived in China, dozens of ZTK-150 drones were being produced before their eyes. They looked strikingly similar to the Iranian-designed Shaheds that Russia deploys in daily terror attacks on Ukrainian cities and communities. The only obvious visual difference was a pair of small canards at the front.
"We visited a very large production facility and saw how everything was done," recalls a member of the team who travelled to China. "We then spent several days negotiating with Chinese intermediaries, until they suggested selling us the technology so we could manufacture everything ourselves. That was when the idea took root: instead of buying and importing drones, we could build them in Ukraine. Those were the first steps towards creating the MICH-2000."
The Ukrainian command was receptive to the idea. However, when the team returned to China to buy the technology, the deal had fallen through: the factory's management had forbidden the sale.
Nevertheless, the Chinese intermediaries were still keen to make the deal happen and found a workaround. Their solution was to assemble the drones elsewhere, where the export restrictions did not apply. The offer also included pilot training, an opportunity the MICH team eagerly took up.
"We went there to train our pilots to fly Chinese drones," a source tells Ukrainska Pravda. "And while the training was underway, we photographed everything we could – from the production process to the arrangement of the shelves and cupboards."
The team returned to Ukraine with eight Chinese-made drones and a group of newly trained pilots.
First test flights
Back home, the team began taking the new drones apart, studying their design and uncovering their flaws. The MICH-2000's first test flight came in the summer of 2024. Its maiden flight lasted only one kilometre before the aircraft crashed because the weight distribution was wrong.
The second test was a step forward: the drone remained airborne for about an hour. But near the end of the flight, one of its propellers came off when vibrations from the engine sheared the bolts that held it in place.
The MICH 2000's first flight
During the third flight, electronic warfare interfered with the drone, revealing another weakness: it was ill-suited to operating amid disrupted communications. Each subsequent launch helped the team identify further changes needed to the design. By the end of the summer, they had mastered airframe production and moved on to experimenting with different electronics.
The company's owner tells Ukrainska Pravda: "When we first began making our own airframes, we made countless mistakes – aerodynamic and structural – and kept running into one problem after another. But every trip to the test range gave us more experience.
For a month and a half, maybe two months, we kept crashing drones at the test range until our client finally said: 'Enough. It's time to put them to work.' We replied that we hadn't even properly got them flying yet – there was always some new problem. But Alpha didn't want to hear it. They wanted results."
A nighttime launch of a MICH 2000
The first combat mission came in October 2024. Three MICH drones were launched: one was shot down, and the other two missed their targets by about 10 m. For Alpha, that was enough. The unit gave the green light for production.
When it comes to aviation, every detail matters
At first glance, the MICH manufacturing plant looks much like any other. But the assembly process has its own peculiarities. It begins with the airframe and the installation of the fuel tank. The MICH is a flying-wing design, meaning it has no separate wings – the aircraft's body performs that function.
The fuel tanks first undergo leak testing. The completed fuselages are then painted black and fed into a specialised robot, which cuts openings for the electronics and other mechanisms. After that, they are sanded, given a final coat of paint and weighed.
Weighing is one of the key quality-control stages. The manufacturer told Ukrainska Pravda that the final weight reveals how accurately the production technology has been followed. Dozens of other checks take place along the way, each governed by its own set of requirements.
The company's owner says: "For me, consistency is everything. The lighter the drone's airframe, the more fuel it can carry, and the less likely it is to run into problems during flight.
Everything we have learned so far shows that there are no small details in manufacturing. A single millimetre out of place, or even a misplaced comma in the code, can cause an error."
After passing the scales, the drones enter the final stage of assembly, where the electronics, motors and combat components are put in place.
In the company's catalogue, there are eight MICH variants designed for either long- or medium-range missions. The MICH can fly up to 2,000 km and carry a payload of 25-60 kg. Operators can select the communications system – analogue, digital, or Starlink – along with the warhead, fuel tank size and guidance assistance for the final stage of the flight.
According to the company, the Chinese MICH and its Ukrainian successor now share little more than an external resemblance. Their prices differ as well: the Chinese predecessor costs US$50,000, while a basic Ukrainian-made MICH costs US$48,000. The final price depends on the configuration – the guidance-assistance system, the number of CRPA antenna channels used to protect navigation against electronic warfare, and other components.
In the past two years, the company has built a network of dozens of manufacturers producing everything from engines, warheads and fuselages to initiation boards, rocket boosters and even the fuel that powers them.
"We had a few painful incidents where third-party boosters destroyed equipment worth US$1 million," the company's owner recalls. "After that, we were no longer allowed to launch aircraft using those boosters. It was probably the most stressful time, because we had only just started developing our own boosters and had not yet tested them in flight.
We knew there was a chance they would not work, but there was no other option. We arrived at the test site and launched the first drone. The booster was not working properly and was producing more thrust than it should. Chemists and engineers spent the night modifying the rockets right there at the site. The next day, the team took part in the launches, and three drones successfully took off. That was when we began scaling up and moving to our own boosters."
Although the company has brought engine and warhead production in-house, it still relies on overseas suppliers for certain components.
CRPA antennas are one example. Only a few companies in Ukraine have mastered their production. Without one, up to 85% of the drone's cost can be localised in Ukraine – that is, covered by domestically sourced components. Once a CRPA antenna is added, that figure drops to 55%. The antennas themselves are expensive, costing as much as US$20,000-25,000 depending on the number of modules.
The MICH 2000's combat path
The company can produce around 6,000 drones a year. Compared with another prominent Ukrainian manufacturer, Fire Point, which has set a target of producing 100,000 drones annually, that figure may seem modest. But there is a reason for the difference.
Unlike the FP-1, which is widely used by various Ukrainian units, the MICH currently has only one user: Alpha.
"We know our drones won't simply disappear into the swamps [Russia]. They will be sent towards a specific target, because Alpha is all about analytics and effectiveness," the company says, demonstrating the analysis behind the strikes.
Ukrainska Pravda has analysed dozens of videos showing attacks on Russian assets using Shahed-like drones. We identified at least eight videos in which the MICH was either in flight or striking its target.
The actual number of MICH strikes is far higher. The company's director says Alpha personnel have launched thousands of the drones, hitting hundreds of targets in both the temporarily occupied territories and Russia.
Since its inception, the MICH has been used in raids on Moscow, destroyed a Tu-95MS strategic bomber at Engels airfield, and struck a logistics hub operated by Russia's largest online retailer, Wildberries, in Ryazan Oblast. It has also destroyed an electronic warfare system used to interfere with Starlink communications in Gelendzhik, near Putin's palace, and taken part in an attack on a naval base of Russia's Baltic Fleet.
The largest-scale MICH strike came at the port of Ust-Luga, where more than 20 drones reached their target.
"During one MICH attack, so many drones made it through to the target that we ran out of targets for them. They started chasing a Pantsir [air defence system] along the road after it had run out of ammunition," the company's director says, laughing.
Most MICH attacks are never captured on camera, but that does not stop the company from monitoring the outcome of each operation through trackers fitted to the drones. The data is then fed back into the development process, helping the team refine the drone's design and software. New changes are introduced almost every week.
MICH 2000 flying in Moscow Oblast
MICH+
The company plans to raise annual production to 10,000 drones in the near future. To make that possible, it is recruiting new staff, seeking additional production sites and expanding its network of suppliers. It is also putting around US$1 million of its monthly profits into R&D.
"We have an R&D department that operates continuously. We conduct trials at the testing ground at least three times a week and work closely with the team," says the company's owner.
The company is currently working on the MICH+, a new medium-range drone that will look different from the MICH-2000 and have no front canards. It is being designed to carry a 70-kg warhead, travel up to 600 km and receive guidance during flight. The expected price is up to US$40,000. The company sees the drone as a way to carve out its own niche in the market.
The company sees organic growth as a more sustainable path than rapid expansion, which can leave production exposed to force majeure events. Growing at a measured pace also gives the company time to build the reserves needed to keep operating if a crisis strikes.
There is also a financial reason for the cautious approach. With essentially just one single customer, the company cannot easily finance a rapid increase in production. It is now looking for additional sources of funding to support expansion.
One option is joint production. The company is considering cooperation with the Baltic states through the Build with Ukraine programme, which could significantly increase drone production with funding from European grants.
"To be honest, I don't want to speculate about what happens after we reach 10,000. I just want the war to end. But if we have to keep working, then we'll keep working," the company's director concludes.

Taliban threaten former Afghan police worker after MoD leak reveals identity
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-16
13:00:28 UTC
22:00:28 KST

A man has received threats from the Taliban after his work for the Afghan police was revealed by a Ministry of Defence leak and the UK refused his application for resettlement.
Hamid* worked for the Afghan national police special unit and received certificates for his work signed by senior British figures praising his “dedication, unparalleled service and leadership”. His details were also included in an accidental 2022 leak by an MoD official that identified 18,700 Afghans who had worked with or for the British government.
Hamid said he had received a number of threats from the Taliban, including a video he shared with the Guardian in which a man cradling a rifle and sitting below a Taliban flag threatens to pursue him and cites knowledge of his previous movements.
The MoD, however, has rejected his application for resettlement under the Afghan relocations and assistance policy (Arap) scheme. His most recent rejection, received on 31 July, stated that Hamid had not provided evidence of “working alongside, in partnership with or closely supporting a UK government department”. It gave him 28 days to appeal.
Hamid said: “This is extremely painful because I have already submitted every document available to me proving my service. Furthermore, many of my former colleagues who served in exactly the same department and performed the same duties have already been relocated to the UK through the Arap scheme.
“Despite this evidence, my case continues to be refused. I believe my case raises serious questions about how some former Afghan partners of the UK continue to be treated despite years of loyal service.”
Hamid’s plea for help comes five years after the Taliban retook power in Afghanistan on 15 August 2021 after the withdrawal of US and Nato forces. The UK government launched the Arap scheme on 1 April 2021 and closed it to new applications on 1 July last year. Pre-existing applications continue to be processed.
Under Arap, high risk of death or serious injury are only taken into account if the rest of the criteria are deemed to have been met, which they have not in Hamid’s case. “Must I wait until I am captured, tortured or killed by the Taliban before my service and the danger I face are finally recognised?” he said.
“Following the Ministry of Defence data breach, my personal information was exposed, placing me at even greater risk. Since then, my life has changed completely. I cannot safely leave my home to work. I live in constant fear of being recognised or targeted.”
After the leak, the then defence secretary, John Healey, said the dataset included people who had made speculative applications under Arap and had not worked with British forces. He said being included in the leak “doesn’t give them a right to claim access to Britain”.
“It doesn’t give them a right to claim asylum. It doesn’t make them eligible for the special [Arap] scheme that Britain put in place for those who’d worked alongside or served with our forces,” he said.
Hamid said that because he was in hiding he had no reliable income and relied on his wife, who supports the family by doing small jobs from home. “This is our family’s only source of income, and even then we struggle simply to survive,” he said.
“The emotional impact has been devastating. My wife and I have become deeply exhausted, depressed and hopeless after years of fear, uncertainty, repeated refusals and financial hardship.
“I am not asking for special treatment. I am only asking for a fair review based on the evidence I have already provided.”
An MoD spokesperson said: “Each application is considered on a case-by-case basis, assessed against the evidence provided, such as how they supported the UK mission in Afghanistan, and in line with the publicly available eligibility criteria.
“Since the Taliban takeover, the UK has resettled almost 39,000 Afghan men, women and children through Afghan resettlement schemes.”

====================================================================================================

‘Our rota crew have the best summer’: parents share how they get through the school holiday
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-16
13:00:26 UTC
22:00:26 KST

The summer holidays are in full swing, bringing the annual challenge many parents face in balancing work and looking after school-age children. With children off school for about 13 weeks a year, but most employees entitled to far less annual leave, parents have told the Guardian that the sums simply do not add up.
New research suggests arranging six weeks of holiday childcare can cost working parents up to £1,145 a child, while almost three-quarters of parents say the summer childcare juggle can damage their career.
We spoke to parents about the creative, and sometimes costly, ways they are making it work.
In Northern Ireland, Emma Willis, 35, relies on flexible working as a stock processor for a charity and her husband’s ability to work from home to get through the summer holidays with their three children, aged 15, 13 and 10.
Willis, who works part-time on minimum wage, says if her husband lost the ability to work from home she would probably have to give up her job.
“I long to work a better job with more hours to enhance all of our lives but right now I have to sit on my hands and keep the plates spinning,” she says. “At the moment, it’s just about getting by. I think that’s what a lot of families are doing – just doing the best they can.”
While the family can manage without paid childcare, she says the children spend much of the holidays at home and she wishes they had more opportunities for activities and trips.
“I feel like our arrangement isn’t great for the kids. They are stuck at home most of the summer and we don’t have the money to engage them in many extracurricular activities.”
It can be harder for those with younger children who are less likely to be able to entertain themselves. Melany Rose, 39, from east London, came up with a radical plan after realising that all her parent friends were taking annual leave on the same day only to meet up in the park.
This inspired her to set up a community childcare rota with nine families.
“There is no point wasting your annual leave allowance just to get through the summer when there’s a creative solution.”
The rota involves 14 children from nine families, though never all at once because families dip in and out depending on trips away and other childcare arrangements. Using a shared spreadsheet, parents take turns, with at least two adults taking the children on adventures to museums, splash parks and other free or low-cost attractions.
The system has eliminated the need for holiday clubs, which can cost £60 a day, and saved families thousands of pounds since they first began.
“Our rota crew have the best summer ever and as adults, we’ve really all bonded. It’s the base of our friendship group now,” she says. “No one gets parent burnout either … six or seven weeks is a long time to be with your kids while you’re trying to juggle working.”
Joe*, from Birmingham, is part of a blended family. He and his wife have a four-year-old together, while he has two other children under 12 who stay with them about 30% of the time, and his wife has a preteen who is with them about 80% of the time.
To cover the six-week summer break, the couple work compressed hours and alternate their non-working days to plug gaps in childcare, using paid holiday clubs only where they feel they are most needed.
He says the biggest challenge is the constant planning. “We have two shared calendars … and we negotiate the summer holidays because we have to work out how we all work, live and keep the kids safe. That’s normally a conversation a few months in advance.”
Diane, 45, from Horsham in West Sussex, gave up her 17-year career in accounts after having children, as she realised the cost of childcare for her son, now 10, and daughter, 7, would leave them financially worse off. Instead she retrained as a school kitchen lead, allowing her to work only in term time, supplementing this with a Saturday retail job.
“I left the profession I worked and trained for and took a complete sidestep into working in school kitchens. It’s less pay, but we’re better off financially.”
Keeping two children entertained still takes weeks of planning, however. Diane relies on free and low-cost council events, booking activities as early as possible before places disappear.
Her son has special educational needs, adding another layer of complexity: “There are a lot of holiday clubs that just won’t take a Send child full stop … Finding support or activities for your child that’s appropriate for your child, it’s an ongoing battle.”
For those who work full-time, the summer holidays can be a huge expense. Jenny, 45, from Newark-on-Trent, and her husband rely on flexible working, annual leave and a patchwork of holiday clubs and activities with their two children, aged six and nine.
To keep track of it all, she has created what she describes as an “epic colour-coded Excel spreadsheet”, mapping out nine different clubs. “Because we’re all over the place I frequently panic that I’m not where I should be,” she says.
When they can, the family uses childcare vouchers, a legacy salary sacrifice scheme not currently open to new applicants that allows participants to pay for registered childcare from pre-tax income. The vouchers covered almost half their paid childcare, but the rest costs about £50 to £60 a day. “We’re dipping into savings,” Jenny says, “but we want them to feel like they’re having a proper holiday.”

How classical musicians experience the sensation of playing together
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-16
13:00:15 UTC
22:00:15 KST

When performing in groups, classical musicians experience a profound sense of shared connection that relies on physical alignment, emotional openness, and specific ensemble skills. A small study published in the Psychology of Music details how performers define this sensation of togetherness, revealing that while musical accuracy matters, reaching peak harmony requires trust and adaptability. The results offer practical guidance for music pedagogy and highlight the social aspects of playing an instrument.
People routinely coordinate their actions in time and space with others. This phenomenon, known as joint action, applies to everyday activities like crossing the street as well as specialized tasks like team sports and dance. Joint actions can provide a sense of joint agency, which researchers define as a feeling of shared control over physical movements and their effects. During successful joint actions, participants often report an optimal state of deep concentration and absorption called flow.
Within musical performances, this shared flow produces a feeling of social and musical connectedness, often referred to as togetherness. Past research has examined togetherness by looking at objective measurements, such as the synchronized breathing, shared head movements, or matched sound intensity of the performers. Sara D’Amario and Laura Bishop, researchers at the University of Oslo, wanted to bridge the gap between these physical measurements and the subjective experiences of the artists. They set out to document how classical musicians consciously perceive their connections with co-performers, as well as the external factors that enhance or disrupt the experience.
The researchers conducted semi-structured phone interviews with 22 advanced music students. The participants included 10 piano students and 12 singing students from the University of Music and Performing Arts Vienna. During the interviews, which lasted an average of 15 minutes, D’Amario asked the participants open-ended questions about their experiences playing in ensembles. The questions prompted the musicians to define togetherness, describe how their repertoire and co-performers influenced the feeling, and share any strategies they used to achieve it.
After transcribing the audio recordings, the researchers used a thematic inductive process to analyze the responses. This method involves reviewing raw text to identify recurring concepts, which researchers then group into broader categories and overarching themes. Both researchers independently coded the transcripts to ensure consistency and minimize the chance of misinterpreting the responses.
Through this analysis, four primary themes emerged regarding how musicians experience togetherness. The first theme centered on the raw sensation of the experience. Participants described togetherness as an embodied feeling, heavily reliant on aligned breathing, synchronized body movements, and eye contact. They characterized these moments as joyful, effortless, and highly rewarding.
The musicians noted that while the sensation is unmistakable when it happens, it remains largely unpredictable and fluctuates throughout a performance. The study distinguished between mechanical precision and deeper emotional synchronization. Some participants described instances of low togetherness as merely vertical. In these cases, the musicians aligned their timing and rhythm with technical accuracy but lacked shared commitment.
High levels of togetherness, described as horizontal, involved true adaptability and a feeling of operating as a single entity. The second theme highlighted the quality of interpersonal relationships that make this horizontal connection possible. The participants indicated that simply playing the right notes at the right time is not enough to establish a strong connection. Performers must share a similar interpretation and emotional understanding of the piece.
The musicians emphasized the necessity of trust and reciprocal responsiveness, meaning they felt free to express themselves because they knew their partner would adapt. Opinions varied on leadership, with some preferring an equal distribution of control and others accepting a clear leader-follower dynamic. As long as both musicians contributed to the shared goal, the specific division of leadership did not prevent the sensation of togetherness.
A third theme focused on the performance setting. Rehearsing generally improved the potential for togetherness, though some participants recalled rare instances of immediate connection without practice. The musicians noted that traditional formal training, such as lessons where a teacher simply accompanies a student, often fails to cultivate this shared focus. Live concerts, by contrast, frequently facilitated high levels of togetherness, as the presence of an audience created an energy exchange that pushed the performers to connect more deeply with the music.
The final theme revolved around specific ensemble skills. The researchers found that an open attitude and a willingness to adapt were essential for musical connection. Instances of poor togetherness usually occurred when a musician focused entirely on their own performance, ignored their partner’s cues, or approached a piece rigidly. To improve group cohesion, the participants recommended that students direct their attention away from the sheet music and actively listen to their co-performers.
Environmental distractors, such as room temperature or background noise, frequently hindered the shared flow. Personal fatigue, bad moods, and a lack of preparation also negatively impacted the ensemble’s ability to sync. The musicians highlighted that external life stressors could easily bleed into the performance space and ruin the delicate balance required for a successful joint action.
The study relies on a small sample of highly skilled classical musicians, meaning the results may not universally apply to amateur players or performers in other musical genres. The participants also conducted the interviews in English, which was not their native language. While they demonstrated a firm grasp of the concepts, conducting the interviews in their primary languages might have yielded more precise descriptions of their emotional states.
The researchers acknowledge that their own professional backgrounds in music and pre-existing ideas about togetherness likely influenced the interview questions and the coding process. Future investigations could involve independent researchers to analyze the data and minimize potential bias. Additionally, upcoming studies will need to combine subjective interviews with physical measurements to see how musicians’ internal feelings map onto bodily processes they cannot consciously control, such as synchronized heart rates.
The study, “Self-reported experiences of togetherness in classical music ensembles,” was authored by Sara D’Amario and Laura Bishop.

Eclipses can set processes in motion whose consequences we do not see immediately. Professional astrologer Kseniia Bazylenko told UNN readers specifically what representatives of each zodiac sign can expect from August 17 to 23.
According to Bazylenko, this period can be called a kind of test.
"But there is no need to be afraid of it. On the contrary, it is worth going through it calmly and with dignity, without unnecessary nerves, rash moves, or the desire to control circumstances at any cost.
If an important decision can be postponed, it is better not to rush. But if events arise independently of you and life itself forces you to make a choice, take it very seriously. Such situations may not be easy, but at the same time they can be of great significance for the future," the astrologer explains.
Bazylenko emphasizes: do not rush. Do not make decisions merely because you are overwhelmed by emotions. Do not try to control absolutely everything. Observe the people, information, and situations that enter your life.

A bright romantic encounter, an important event in a child’s life, a return to a creative project, or unexpected recognition of your talent is possible.

Islamic-era industrial complex in the middle of nowhere, Ramat Gan puzzles archaeologists
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-16
12:52:40 UTC
21:52:40 KST

Normally, shopping and manufacturing complexes are located in or on the outskirts of cities. That is true today and applied in antiquity too.
Beneath the parking lot of Winter Stadium in the central Israeli city of Ramat Gan ahead of the construction of a bus terminal, archaeologists have discovered some sort of industrial-commercial complex from the Islamic period, the late seventh century to the early ninth century, the Israel Antiquities Authority announced on Sunday. The puzzle is that they haven't found any city or even a small settlement connected with it, Dr. Yoav Arbel, co-director of the excavation on behalf of the IAA together with Lior Rauchberger, tells Haaretz.
What did they find? A bird's-eye view suggests the complex, which operated for about 150 years, had been planned: It features two straight, intersecting streets along which are rooms, which the archaeologists believe served as shops or warehouses, or workshops. Of these, all that remains are mostly the foundations, and some walls.
Though Israel by and large is riddled with archaeological finds going back almost 2 million years, well before the dawn of Homo sapiens and empire, and Ramat Gan is located in a very inviting area for habitation, these may be the oldest streets ever found in Ramat Gan, the archaeologists add.
Note that they aren't the only archaeological remains ever found in Ramat Gan, technically a city located east of Tel Aviv, though the urban landscape is consecutive. Ramat Gan also boasts Tel Gerisa (aka Napoleon's Hill, from which Napoleon did not snipe at Jaffa, despite local legends) on the banks of the Yarkon River, dating to the Bronze Age, for example.
Another startling archaeological find in the city was that the Ramat Gan Safari zoo had unwittingly been using a Roman sarcophagus to grow geraniums for some 25 years.
Back underneath the Winter parking lot, the excavation has found no evidence of residence, Arbel says, at last not in its main phase of usage. The rooms they uncovered could have been storerooms or shops in the phase from the late seventh century to the early ninth, when the site was abandoned. In other words, the site seems to have been a stand-alone industrial-commercial complex.
"We have no sign there was a city," he spells out. "We have industrial and commercial complexes in other areas, always in cities or on their margins, but this seems to have been an independent complex." Nor do they know any history of any major settlement where Winter Stadium stands today, home to the Hakoach Amidar Ramat Gan soccer club.
We just add that the Winter Stadium in Ramat Gan doesn't feature cold-weather sports, but is named for its builders: the clothing manufacturer Jack and his wife, Muriel Winter.
The archaeologists' best explanation at this point is this complex was the ancient equivalent of a big roadside service area, a travel stop: It was very close to the roads connecting Jaffa and Ramle with Jerusalem. "It's strange," Arbel sums up. "We never found anything like this that wasn't part of a city. Maybe there is a settlement we haven't found yet."
Possibly there had been a settlement whose walls were nicked. After its first abandonment, for about two generations, the archaeologists estimate – its walls were dismantled and the materials were repurposed.
Whatever it was, this facility operated for about 150 years until being abandoned in the late ninth century. The site was resettled after a couple of generations, Arbel says, in roughly the mid-10th or early 11th century, from which time they do find evidence of residence. Then it was abandoned again in the 11th century, before the Crusader invasion.
Why would a well-situated site, which likely had water sources even if they haven't been located yet, be abandoned? "The first time around, we don't know," Arbel says, but clearly, abandoned it had been. The archaeologists don't know why it was abandoned the second time around either, but speculate that it was possibly because of the political turmoil that marked the late Islamic period in the Holy Land – or natural disaster.
Israel sits smack on the Dead Sea system of faults and there were a lot of earthquakes in the 11th century, Arbel points out, some of them devastating. In any case, the site was never resettled, the archaeologists say, leaving aside the construction of modern Israel and the Winter Stadium parking lot on the very spot.
Who used the site? We don't know – the first phase dates to the Umayyad and Abbasid periods, and the later residential settlement existed during the Fatimid period. But the pottery, glass, coins and other artifacts found there shed no helpful light on occupants; during the Islamic period Israel had a diverse population.
"Ramle, the district capital, had a Muslim community, while the Yarkon region was probably home to many Samaritans — descendants of a large population that flourished in the area during the Byzantine period, which preceded the Muslim conquest in the seventh century C.E.," the archaeologists point out. But they found nothing that could point to the ethnic or religious identity of people in this anomalous industrial zone that had no city.

21:49:25 KST

PHNOM PENH, Aug. 16 (Xinhua) -- Around 500 cyclists took to the roads on Sunday, completing a 179-kilometer journey across Cambodia to promote green tourism and deliver educational supplies to underprivileged students.
The event drew both local and international cyclists from various countries. The group journeyed from the capital city of Phnom Penh to Phnom Da Temple, a major historical tourism site located in the southern province of Takeo.
Speaking at the event, Cambodian Minister of Tourism Huot Hak highlighted how the initiative blends athletics with community impact, noting that the event showcases a unique tourism product connecting sports, heritage, nature, the environment, and local communities.
"This combination creates fresh experiences, stimulates both domestic and international travel, and helps establish Takeo province as a vibrant destination, particularly during the Green Season," he said.
The event aims to stimulate tourist flows during the Green Season and contribute to social initiatives through the donation of educational materials to underprivileged students, he added.
The cycling journey kicked off at Phnom Penh's Independence Monument Roundabout and headed into Takeo Province. Along the way, participants passed through several key areas and tourist sites, including Tonle Bati, Phnom Chisor, Ang Tasom, and Angkor Borei district, before arriving at their final destination, Phnom Da Temple.
Cycling is not only a form of physical exercise that promotes both physical and mental well-being, but also a tourism activity that enables participants to directly experience nature, traditions, customs, local ways of life, and communities along the route, Hak said.
Upon reaching Phnom Da Temple, the cyclists participated in a green initiative, planting 600 peacock flower trees along both sides of the road leading to the historic site.
This practical initiative contributes to promoting a greener environment and enhancing the beauty of the tourism area, Hak said.
Tourism remains one of Cambodia's four economic pillars, alongside agriculture, construction and real estate, and manufacturing exports. However, the nation welcomed just 1.75 million foreign visitors in the first half of this year, a 47.9 percent drop from the 3.36 million recorded during the same period last year.
Hak attributed this sharp downturn to compounding challenges, including negative publicity, technology-enabled scam networks, border friction with Thailand, and Middle Eastern geopolitical conflicts that have driven up fuel prices and dampened international travel demand. ■
