Physicists discover a hidden gluon structure inside protons that could rewrite textbooks
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-16
09:55:45 UTC
18:55:45 KST

Physicists discover a hidden gluon structure inside protons that could rewrite textbooks
- Date:
- August 16, 2026
- Source:
- Brookhaven National Laboratory
- Summary:
- Physicists may have uncovered a hidden feature inside protons that helps preserve one of matter’s most fundamental properties. RHIC collision data suggest baryon number is carried not simply by three quarks, but by a Y-shaped junction of the gluons connecting them. The finding challenges a decades-old textbook picture and could deepen our understanding of why protons—and ultimately matter itself—remain stable.
- Share:
New findings from the STAR detector at the Relativistic Heavy Ion Collider (RHIC) are challenging a familiar picture of what gives protons one of their defining quantum properties. The results suggest that gluons, the particles that act as the glue holding quarks together, may play a key role in carrying and conserving baryon number.
The evidence comes from high-energy particle collisions at RHIC, a U.S. Department of Energy (DOE) Office of Science user facility for nuclear physics research that operated at DOE's Brookhaven National Laboratory from 2000 to early 2026. According to the new study, published in Science, baryon number may be associated with a Y-shaped "junction" of gluons connecting the proton's three main quarks. If confirmed, that would challenge the long-standing assumption that baryon number belongs exclusively to those quarks.
"Traditionally, scientists have assumed that each of the three main 'valence' quarks inside a proton or neutron carries one-third of the baryon number," said Zhangbu Xu, a professor at Kent State University with a joint appointment at Brookhaven Lab.
A Decades-Old Idea About Gluons
Physicists first proposed the baryon junction, also called a gluon junction, in the 1970s as a way to describe how gluons connect the valence quarks inside a proton. In 1996, four years before RHIC began operating, Dmitri Kharzeev, a theoretical physicist at Stony Brook University and Brookhaven Lab, proposed that this junction might do something even more fundamental. Rather than the valence quarks carrying baryon number, the junction itself could be responsible.
The STAR collaboration has now developed a way to test that possibility using several types of collisions produced at RHIC.
"Using data collected from different types of particle collisions at RHIC, our results suggest that the baryon number is not simply carried by individual quarks," Xu added. "Our findings strongly support the idea that baryon number is more favorably carried and transported by gluons, the particles that hold quarks together, when arranged in this special configuration."
Why Baryon Number Matters
Determining what actually carries baryon number matters far beyond the internal structure of a proton. In RHIC collisions, conservation of baryon number means that the total number of baryons, three-quark particles such as protons and neutrons, must remain unchanged before and after the collision. The same conservation principle also applies on the scale of the universe.
"Since the Big Bang, the number of protons and neutrons all together never changes as a function of time," said Nicole Lewis, a STAR physicist at Rice University who started this project as a postdoc at Brookhaven Lab in 2020. "The reasons for this conservation are not well understood. It's one of the mysteries of the universe, related to why we have more matter than antimatter," she said.
Baryon number conservation also has a much more tangible consequence. It helps explain the extraordinary stability of protons, which form a central part of atomic nuclei and do not appear to decay under ordinary circumstances.
"It's believed that the lifetime of a proton is longer than the lifespan of the universe," Lewis said. "This allows atomic nuclei to form and be stable -- which means matter, as we interact with it in the universe, can exist."
A More Complicated Proton
The possibility that gluons carry baryon number would overturn the standard simplified description found in many textbooks. In that picture, a proton has a baryon number of plus one, divided equally among its three main valence quarks. Each quark therefore carries plus one third of the baryon number, much as the proton's electric charge is distributed among its three valence quarks.
But real protons are much more complicated than that simplified model suggests.
"In the naïve quark model, there are three quarks inside a proton, but nothing else," said Tommy Tsang, formerly a postdoc at Kent State University, now at DOE's Argonne National Laboratory. "But if we look at details inside, there are not only three quarks but also a lot of gluons interacting, connecting between those quarks, and there are also quarks and antiquarks that pop up from the vacuum, so it's actually a really complex object."
Quantum chromodynamics (QCD), the theory used to describe these interactions, has been highly successful in explaining the strong force that acts among quarks and gluons. Even so, models inspired by QCD often need additional assumptions to reproduce some of the particle patterns observed when RHIC smashes nuclei together at nearly the speed of light.
An Unexpected Excess of Baryons
One observation in particular caught the STAR team's attention. The detector repeatedly records more baryons than antibaryons emerging sideways from the collisions, perpendicular to the direction of the incoming beams.
"In the STAR detector, we consistently see an excess of baryons coming out of the collisions perpendicular to the direction of the colliding beams," Tsang said. "The fact that we end up with more baryons than antibaryons -- or more matter than antimatter -- is not surprising since our collisions start with matter," he said.
These extremely energetic collisions convert tremendous amounts of energy into thousands of newly created particles. What puzzled the researchers was not simply that more baryons than antibaryons were produced. It was where the excess baryons appeared.
If valence quarks alone carried the baryon number, explaining the excess away from the beamline would require all three valence quarks from one colliding proton to stop near the center of the detector. They would then have to undergo a conversion from matter into energy and back into matter, producing new baryons that move outward perpendicular to the beam.
The STAR researchers suspected there might be another explanation.
Electric Charge Provides a Test
The team found a way to investigate the mystery by taking advantage of another property of valence quarks: electric charge. Scientists compared the net baryon number measured in different RHIC nuclear collisions with the way electric charge was redistributed in those same events.
"Measuring the electric charge coming out perpendicular to the collision gives you a definitive way of measuring how many quarks are stopped and transformed into new particles," said Zebo Tang, a professor at the University of Science and Technology of China who led a group of students performing data analyses and model simulations.
The comparison revealed a striking mismatch. Researchers observed roughly twice as many baryons as should have been produced based on the electric charge associated with stopped quarks.
According to models based on QCD, that means too few quarks were being stopped to account for all the baryons appearing in the detector.
That left an important question: What was carrying the extra baryon number?
The STAR physicists argue that gluons offer a possible answer, specifically the three-pronged gluon junction that connects the proton's valence quarks.
How the Gluon Junction Could Carry Baryon Number
The proposed mechanism depends on what happens when protons inside colliding nuclei reach enormous energies. According to the STAR team, the "gluon junction" or "baryon junction" that links the quarks may be much easier to stop in a collision than the three quarks themselves.
If the junction is stopped, its energy can be converted into newly produced baryons that travel outward in directions perpendicular to the beams. Meanwhile, the valence quarks that were previously connected by the junction can continue moving forward along the beampipe.
Understanding why requires looking at the changing internal structure of a proton as its energy increases.
"The baryon junction is always there even as protons are accelerated to higher and higher energy," Prithwish Tribedy, a STAR physicist at Brookhaven Lab. "But at high energy, gluons within the proton split and multiply."
As the number of gluons increases, the proton's momentum becomes spread among more of them. Each individual gluon, including those forming the junction, therefore carries a smaller portion of the proton's total momentum. The valence quarks, however, continue to carry much of the proton's forward motion.
As a result, when the collision occurs, the comparatively slower three-pronged gluon junction should be easier to stop and convert into new particles than the rapidly moving quarks.
Stopping one connected structure is also simpler than stopping three separate quarks, making such an interaction more likely, according to Tribedy.
"In the collision, the baryon junction gets held behind, and the quarks continue on," he noted.
Building New Particles After the Collision
Quarks and gluons cannot remain isolated, so after the collision they quickly combine with other particles.
In a simplified example, a quark continuing down the beampipe could join with an antiquark and form a two-quark particle called a meson. At the same time, the three-pronged gluon junction could behave somewhat like a Y-shaped magnet, drawing in three newly created quarks from the vacuum and producing a new baryon.
Actual RHIC collisions are considerably more violent and complex.
"Even though we start with nuclei that contain roughly 100 protons and 100 neutrons, these collisions create thousands of new particles; 99% of the energy is transformed into new particles," said Rongrong Ma, a Brookhaven Lab physicist.
The STAR team found that collisions producing larger numbers of particles also showed a greater excess of "midrapidity" baryons compared with predictions based on the simpler picture in which quarks alone carry baryon number.
The fact that so many of these baryons emerge perpendicular to the beamline provides strong evidence, according to the researchers, that the baryon junction exists and plays an important role in transporting baryon number.
Rethinking a Fundamental Property of Matter
The results suggest that one of the proton's defining quantum properties may not reside solely in its three valence quarks. Instead, the gluon structure connecting those quarks could be central to how baryon number is carried through energetic collisions.
"Our research challenges the long-held idea that baryon number is simply divided among and carried by the three quarks," said Ma. "This new understanding reshapes how we think about the structure of matter and deepens our knowledge of the most fundamental element that is responsible for the universe in its current form."
The research was supported by the DOE Office of Science, the U.S. National Science Foundation (NSF), and numerous international agencies and organizations listed in the scientific paper. Researchers also used the Open Science Grid, which is supported directly by NSF, along with computing resources at Brookhaven Lab's Scientific Data and Computing Facilities and the National Energy Research Scientific Computing Center (NERSC), another DOE Office of Science user facility located at DOE's Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory.

Flags to fly at half-staff in Hong Kong as tribute to late ex-premier Zhu Rongji
Flags will be lowered on Tuesday at government headquarters, Government House, border crossings and Hong Kong airport
Hong Kong will fly the national and regional flags at half-staff at various government sites on Tuesday to mourn the late former Chinese premier Zhu Rongji.
The government said on Sunday it would lower the flags at government headquarters in Admiralty, Government House, all control points and checkpoints at border crossings and Hong Kong International Airport.
The tribute will be paid on the day of Zhu’s cremation, in accordance with a notice issued by state news agency Xinhua.
It said that the national flag would also be flown at half-staff at various sites across the country, including Tiananmen Square, Xinhua Gate, the Great Hall of the People and the Ministry of Foreign Affairs in Beijing.

Parliament at a standstill, protests on streets: The Monsoon session story
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-16
09:53:12 UTC
18:53:12 KST

Parliament at a standstill, protests on streets: The Monsoon session story
Abhishek Mishra / TIMESOFINDIA.COM / Updated: Aug 16, 2026, 18:27 IST
Comments
Share
AA
Text Size
Small
Medium
Large
19% in Lok Sabha, 39% in Rajya Sabha: How Monsoon Session unfolded beyond the Parliament
NEW DELHI: For 25 days, Parliament’s Monsoon Session played out on two different stages.Inside the Houses, proceedings were repeatedly disrupted, adjournments were frequent and Question Hour had barely any time remaining. Outside, political activity rarely stopped. Students marched, opposition leaders protested, ministers traded charges, and the Parliament complex itself became a stage for demonstrations and symbolic political performances.Held from July 20 to August 13, the session produced an unusual contrast: legislation moved forward, but much of the political confrontation surrounding it played out beyond the floor of the two Houses.
The numbers underline that contrast. Lok Sabha functioned for approximately 19% of its scheduled time, while Rajya Sabha functioned for around 39%. Question Hour was particularly badly hit, with less than 1% of its scheduled time utilised. The session had 19 sittings spread over 25 days.Parliamentary affairs minister Kiren Rijiju acknowledged the distinction between legislative output and debate.“It was a good session…we have passed 13 bills; but it was not a good session in terms of discussion,” he said, while accusing the opposition of avoiding debate despite the government's willingness to discuss issues.
'Not a good session in terms of discussion'
Yet government business did move, much of it through voice votes amid opposition sloganeering.
Bills passed in Parliament
Eleven Bills were introduced in Lok Sabha and two in Rajya Sabha. Twelve Bills were passed by Lok Sabha and 12 by Rajya Sabha, with 12 Bills cleared by both Houses during the session.Two Bills replacing and incorporating the provisions of ordinances issued before the session, the Supreme Court (Number of Judges) Amendment Ordinance, 2026 and the Income-Tax (Amendment) Ordinance, 2026, were also passed by both Houses.The Demands for Excess Grants for 2022-23 were taken up, with the related Appropriation Bill passed by Lok Sabha on August 4 and returned by Rajya Sabha on August 6. The Foreign Contribution (Regulation) Amendment Bill, 2026 was referred to a Joint Committee for examination.Among the more politically significant measures was the Public Examinations (Prevention of Unfair Means) Amendment Bill, 2026, introduced amid concerns over public examinations and paper leaks.
Bills passed by both the Houses
The Bill came after Prime Minister Narendra Modi announced stringent measures to prevent such incidents in the future, including multiple selfie videos directly addressing students.It provides for speedy investigations and time-bound trials, with investigations to be completed within two months and trials within three months. It also provides for Special Fast Track Courts and Special Public Prosecutors, allows the Centre to constitute Special Task Forces where necessary, enhances penalties and creates a time-bound appellate mechanism before a Division Bench of the High Court.The Bill was passed by both Houses and received presidential assent.Its debate also offered a glimpse of how political parties were trying to speak directly to younger voters. BJP’s younger leaders took the lead in explaining the legislation and the Centre’s position, while the opposition made its own pitch. Both sides adopted Gen Z vocabulary, trading barbs with phrases such as “clock it”, “FOMO” and “delulu”.Other major Bills passed during the session included the Prevention of Insults to National Honour (Amendment) Bill, which seeks to bring Vande Mataram within the ambit of the 1971 Act; the Registration of Births and Deaths (Amendment) Bill, which proposes stricter procedures for delayed registration; and the MSME Development (Amendment) Bill, which provides for a national digital platform for voluntary registration and seeks to improve access to finance and resolve delayed-payment disputes faster.
Bills passed in this Monsoon Session
The Bankers' Books Evidence Bill expands the definition of bankers' books to cover physical, electronic, digital, virtual and cloud-based records. The Kerala (Alteration of Name) Bill proposes changing the state’s name from Kerala to Keralam. Other legislation dealt with cooperative development, tribunals and the mining sector.But these measures were not what defined the political atmosphere of the session. That distinction belonged to the protests outside.
The session began with a protest
The Monsoon Session opened against the backdrop of a large student mobilisation at Jantar Mantar over NEET examination irregularities.The protest had been building for weeks. Scientist and activist Sonam Wangchuk had been on a hunger strike for more than 20 days when the Centre intervened and removed him from the protest site.His removal intensified the agitation, with students going ahead with their scheduled “Sansad gherao”. Security personnel, including the Rapid Action Force and Delhi Police, were deployed as the protesters marched towards Parliament.The distance was less than 1.5 km, but the march quickly turned into a major confrontation.Pellet guns, lathi-charge and tear gas were used, with more than 60 people injured and admitted to nearby Lady Hardinge Medical College and Ram Manohar Lohia Hospital.The police action immediately became a political issue, with opposition leaders turning their focus towards Union home minister Amit Shah because the security forces involved came under the home ministry’s jurisdiction.The student protests subsequently spread beyond Delhi. The pressure group Cockroach Janta Party’s delegation met PM Modi-led cabinet ministers Jagat Prakash Nadda and Jitendra Singh, after which the situation moved towards normalcy.One of the protesters’ major demands was the removal of Dharmendra Pradhan as education minister.On July 25, Pradhan resigned from the post, making his departure one of the defining political developments of the session.
From Pradhan to Shah
Pradhan’s resignation did not end the political confrontation.Lok Sabha leader of opposition Rahul Gandhi had not joined the initial Jantar Mantar protest but emerged as a prominent voice in the political battle that followed. His focus shifted from Pradhan to Shah, whom he repeatedly attacked over the police crackdown on students on July 20.“As home minister, did you approve the use of lethal force including pellet guns against students? If not, who did? Are the people in plainclothes seen beating students with lathis police personnel or volunteers? Youth and students, future of our country, are demanding answers and accountability,” Rahul said.
Rahul Gandhi trains guns at Amit Shah
He argued that Shah either directly ordered the use of pellet guns, shock batons, lathicharge and tear gas, making him “culpable” for the treatment of the protesters, or did not know what the police were doing, making him “incompetent”.“In either case, he has to go,” Rahul said, calling on Prime Minister Narendra Modi to sack the home minister.Rahul also alleged that students were facing threats, including through face recognition and Bajrang Dal. “These are our children and the govt has no business threatening them or beating them. They have not committed any crime. They should not be punished,” he said.He later made the demand for Shah’s removal explicit, saying: “Shah is responsible and we are not going to let him get away with it.”At the AICC headquarters, with Shah’s photograph displayed on a large screen, Rahul accused the home minister of being responsible for the treatment of students and criticised his absence from Lok Sabha, saying it showed that he was “guilty”.Inside Parliament, opposition leaders across parties continued to seek answers from Shah and Prime Minister Narendra Modi. The issue contributed to repeated disruptions.The government, meanwhile, maintained that Shah was ready to discuss the student protests.
The debate that moved between the House and outside
In the final week of the session, Shah offered to address the opposition’s concerns directly.He offered to sit in Parliament from “3pm till 3pm the next day” to hear the opposition and respond to its points. Rahul rejected the offer, saying they “seek answers, not lectures”.Shah’s offer came amid demands that he make a statement in Parliament on the police action during the July 20 march over the NEET paper leak.He later wrote to Lok Sabha Speaker Om Birla seeking time for a discussion on the student protest and NEET paper leak.
Monsoon Session
“As you are aware, Hon’ble parliamentary affairs minister Shri Kiren Rijiju has agreed, on behalf of the government, to a discussion in Parliament on the student movement concerning the NEET examination, during the meeting of the Business Advisory Committee,” Shah said.He also pointed out that the Lok Sabha had already discussed the Public Examinations (Prevention of Unfair Means) Amendment Bill during the session, but opposition MPs had not raised the NEET examination issue during that debate.The exchange captured the central political tension of the session.The government pointed to its legislative response and willingness to debate. The opposition demanded direct answers over the handling of the protests and accountability for the police action.The argument was therefore no longer simply about an examination paper leak. It had become a contest over responsibility, policing and ministerial accountability, much of it fought outside the chamber.
Jharkhand adds another layer
Examination irregularities also became a political issue in Jharkhand, where the Centre’s political opponents were in power.Students in the state protested over alleged irregularities in competitive examinations, including JPSC and JSSC, under the Hemant Soren government.In Ranchi, protesters marched towards the state assembly in an “assembly gherao”. The Soren government said it was open to talks and held rounds of discussions with student delegations.For the BJP at the Centre, the Jharkhand protests provided an opportunity to counter Rahul Gandhi’s attacks over the student movement in Delhi.Pradhan, days after resigning as education minister, turned his fire on Rahul.“The leader of opposition, who habitually lies, neither wants to come to Parliament nor listen to answers. They just want to spread their lies and shed crocodile tears,” Pradhan said.
Pradhan calls Rahul Gandhi a 'habitual liar'
He also accused Rahul of making “baseless, factless false accusations” against Shah.The political irony was clear: the examination issue that had put the Union government under pressure in Delhi was now being used by the BJP to target the Congress, which is part of the ruling alliance with the Jharkhand Mukti Morcha government led by Hemant Soren.
Then came the Ram Mandir protest
The student protests showed how street mobilisation could shape parliamentary politics. Another demonstration showed how the Parliament complex itself could become a stage for political messaging.The alleged theft of donations at the Ram Mandir in Ayodhya became another opposition issue during the session.On Friday, Independent MP Pappu Yadav, along with other opposition MPs, staged a symbolic protest at Makar Dwar over the alleged embezzlement of Ram Temple donations. Congress president Mallikarjun Kharge, Rahul Gandhi, Priyanka Gandhi Vadra, Samajwadi Party MPs Awadhesh Prasad and Dharmendra Yadav, and Jharkhand Mukti Morcha MP Mahua Maji participated.The MPs held placards and a large banner reading “Amit Shah Sadan Se Gayab Kyun?” They also raised slogans demanding Shah’s resignation and his presence in the House.Pappu Yadav, whose real name is Rajesh Ranjan, dressed as a temple priest carrying a photograph of Lord Ram and sat beside donation boxes. Opposition MPs acted as devotees and placed money in the box. Yadav then symbolically slipped the money into his pocket, representing the opposition’s allegation of theft.Videos circulating online also showed Rahul Gandhi putting money into the donation box. Another MP, playing a devotee, confronted the “priest” over the alleged act.The priest denied wrongdoing before theatrically leaving the scene. The INDIA bloc said the demonstration was intended to highlight the alleged embezzlement of Ram Temple donations and demand accountability from the Centre.It was a symbolic protest, but it reflected the broader character of the session: political messaging increasingly spilled into the physical spaces around Parliament.
A Parliament that worked, but talked less
The Monsoon Session cannot simply be described as one in which Parliament failed to function. Bills were introduced and passed, financial business was completed, ordinances were replaced and the Public Examinations (Prevention of Unfair Means) Amendment Bill became law.But the productivity figures tell another story. Lok Sabha functioned for approximately 19% of its scheduled time, while Rajya Sabha functioned for around 39%.Inside the Houses, protests and sloganeering repeatedly led to adjournments. Key government Bills were passed, often through voice votes. Outside, meanwhile, Parliament’s premises became venues for demonstrations and political performances.That contrast defined the session.The Jantar Mantar protest became a parliamentary issue. The police action turned into a political battle over Amit Shah. Pradhan’s resignation followed sustained pressure over the examination controversy. The same issue travelled to Jharkhand, where it became another weapon in the Centre’s political contest with the opposition. The Ram Mandir controversy then produced a symbolic demonstration inside the Parliament complex.
In each case, the politics extended beyond the floor of the House.The Monsoon Session thus offered an unusual picture of parliamentary politics: legislation continued inside, while confrontation, mobilisation and political messaging increasingly took place outside. The Houses passed 12 Bills, but some of the session’s most visible battles were fought through protests, slogans, press statements, letters and demonstrations.Parliament was still working. But it was talking less, while the political argument increasingly moved beyond its walls.On August 13, both Houses adjourned sine die and will meet again in the Winter Session.
Abhishek Mishra is a Digital Content Producer at The Times of India, working with the news desk. He writes with a keen eye on foreign policy, defence developments, and the shifting currents of geopolitics-and yes, Indian politics always finds a way onto his radar too.

Corgis run, bark and sniff their way to glory at a growing international race
VILNIUS, Lithuania (AP) — It’s not all about short-legged speed when 150 corgis gather for an international race celebrating the little dogs. There’s a costume parade, the “smartest nose,” and — of course — the loudest bark.
The fifth Corgi Race Vilnius drew dogs and their owners to the Lithuanian capital’s Vingis park on Saturday for what organizers said was the biggest edition yet. There were competitors from Lithuania, Latvia, Poland, Estonia, Germany, Ukraine, the Czech Republic, the United States and Britain — the country most closely associated with the breed, famously a favorite of the late Queen Elizabeth II.
“In the first year, we gathered 40 corgis from one city. This year, it’s 150 from nine countries, and for the first time we have a participant from the place where the breed originated,” organizer Edvinas Miskas said.
“We call Vilnius the European capital of corgis, and when people from the breed’s homeland start coming to us rather than the other way around, that title begins to sound a little more serious.”
Ninety-four dogs took part in the main running event, competing in qualifiers, semifinals and the final.
In the final, which pitted corgis against each other over 25 meters (82 feet), the winner was American competitor GG, short for Gustave the Girl Dog. Another U.S. entrant, Mr. Corgington, finished a close second. Lithuania’s own Moka, a two-time former champion, was third.
But much of the program dispensed with speed to explore the other skills of the dogs — and their owners.
There was a costume parade featuring 38 corgis in diverse outfits including a dinosaur suit, a dress and doggy sports gear. Amigo swept both the four-judge jury and the public Facebook vote for a flawless costume entry with a knight-like look.
In the “smartest nose” challenge, dogs searched for hidden treats. Latvian corgis Tora and Rusty shared the win.
And then there was the loudest bark competition. The first British competitor, 12-year-old Pembroke Welsh corgi Duke from Sedbergh in northwest England, didn’t participate in the main race because of his stately age but was a hopeful in the barking stakes after, as his owner put it, training for his whole life.
It was Mr. Corgington who won the loudest bark contest, though.
He was one of the most traveled competitors. The final race offered him a rematch after he finished second against GG at a major race at Emerald Downs in Auburn, Washington — her second consecutive win there.
Half of the corgis registered in Vilnius this year were taking part for the first time. But six veterans — costume winner Amigo, Foksas, Foksis, Madeira, Bulka and Dziugas — have attended every edition.

12:52:42 EEST
18:52:42 KST

Finland’s Alisa Vainio won the women’s marathon at the European Athletics Championships in Birmingham on Sunday, finishing almost five minutes ahead of her nearest rival and setting a championship record of 2:22:26. The 28-year-old led from the opening stages and completed most of the race alone.
Vainio finished four minutes and 55 seconds ahead of Hungary’s Lili Anna Vindics-Tóth, who took silver in 2:27:21.
Britain’s Abbie Donnelly won bronze in 2:27:33, five minutes and seven seconds behind the winner.
The margin was the largest recorded in the women’s marathon at the European Championships, according to Yle. The previous record belonged to Portugal’s Rosa Mota, who won by four minutes and 14 seconds.
Vainio also lowered the championship record by almost three minutes on a Birmingham course featuring hills, turns and repeated five-kilometre laps through the city centre. The previous record stood at 2:25:20.
She separated from the field within the opening kilometre and continued at her own pace as the gap increased. At 20 kilometres she led by about three minutes. The advantage reached three and a half minutes at 25 kilometres and exceeded four minutes by 30 kilometres.
Vainio passed 35 kilometres in 1:57:37 and reached 40 kilometres in 2:14:49 before completing the race without a late challenge.
After the finish, she told Yle that she had intended to begin at a comfortable pace and continued when nobody followed.
“I thought I would start by running relaxed,” Vainio said in the interview. “When nobody came with me, I thought I would just keep running relaxed.”
She said the result had not yet sunk in and credited her family and coach for supporting her preparation.
“This ranks quite high among the marathons I have run,” she told Yle. “There has been a lot of work behind this.”
Vainio’s victory gave Finland its first European title in the women’s marathon.
The European Athletics Championships conclude in Birmingham on Sunday evening, with Finland’s Juho Alasaari due to compete in the men’s pole vault final.

World Archery just reinstated Russia’s flag and anthem, despite its killing more than 760 Ukrainian athletes and coaches since 2022
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-16
09:51:22 UTC
18:51:22 KST

An international sports body has welcomed Russia back under its flag while Russia keeps killing Ukraine's athletes and civilians. The World Archery Federation has lifted restrictions on Russian athletes, allowing them to compete with their country's identity, including under the Russian flag and anthem, the federation announced.
Russia has killed more than 760 Ukrainian athletes and coaches since the start of the full-scale war, with many others made refugees or losing loved ones to strikes on civilians, and some who took up arms without combat experience. Among them is Ukrainian archer Oleksandr Onyshchuk, a master of sport and European champion, killed fighting the occupiers.
What World Archery decided
The federation acted on an Olympic ruling. Its Executive Board met online on 14 August to review the International Olympic Committee's (IOC) 7 July decision, which confirmed that earlier recommendations restricting Russian athletes no longer applied, then lifted the restrictions on Russian athletes, teams, and officials at its events.
The Russians may now compete fully. They can take part under their national flag and anthem at events including the Archery World Cup and World Championships, and the 2022 restrictions on the Russian flag and anthem were removed, in line with a similar decision on Belarus in May. The federation said participation remains subject to standard eligibility, anti-doping, host-country, and visa requirements, and that it supports the Ukrainian archery community and all affected by the war.
Ukraine calls it sportswashing
For Ukraine, the reinstatement serves Russia's propaganda. Allowing Russian athletes into international competition is a means of sportswashing, spreading disinformation, and legitimizing the aggression against Ukraine before foreign audiences, while presenting Russia as still part of the civilized world.
Ukraine also points to who Russia sends. Ukrainian intelligence has documented Russian athletes who are direct participants in the war, including a lieutenant colonel in Russia's armed forces and a deputy brigade commander who competed internationally, according to Ukraine's Defense Intelligence.
Ukraine's National Olympic Committee called the IOC decision behind the reinstatement premature and unjustified and has appealed it to the Court of Arbitration for Sport. The archery ruling arrives as Russia's strikes keep killing Ukrainian civilians and athletes in the war that the returning competitors' flag represents.

The matter was scheduled for hearing after the Supreme Court said on August 12.
NEW DELHI: The Supreme Court is set to hear on Monday the Tamil Nadu government's plea seeking directions to Karnataka to release its due share of Cauvery water immediately.The case is listed before a bench of Justices Vikram Nath and Sandeep Mehta, according to the court's cause list for August 17.The matter was scheduled for hearing after the Supreme Court said on August 12 that petitions filed by Tamil Nadu and others, including the DMK, would be taken up on August 17.
Tamil Nadu approached the top court on August 3, arguing that it was not receiving its allocated share of Cauvery water despite the state facing a rain-deficient year.The state government has alleged that both the quantity recommended for release by the Cauvery Water Regulation Committee and the actual water supplied by Karnataka were far below its requirement.ALSO READ | Mekedatu project long-term solution to Cauvery water dispute: Minister
Tamil Nadu flags shortfall in water release
At a meeting on July 28, the Cauvery Water Regulation Committee directed Karnataka to release 3,500 cusecs of water to Tamil Nadu for 15 days from July 29.Tamil Nadu, however, said the actual flow recorded at Biligundlu on the Karnataka-Tamil Nadu border was only between 158 and 550 cusecs from July 29 to August 2.The state government also pointed to water storage levels in Karnataka's four reservoirs. As of August 3, the combined storage in the Krishna Raja Sagara, Kabini, Harangi and Hemavathy reservoirs was 77.537 TMC, according to a Tamil Nadu government statement.
Tamil Nadu argued that Karnataka would be able to release its due share without facing difficulty.
State claims 26.954 TMC is due
Tamil Nadu said recent rainfall in the catchment areas of the KRS and Kabini reservoirs had increased the amount of water that should flow to the state.
According to the state government, the proportionate quantity due at Biligundlu should be 26.954 TMC."Accordingly, the Cauvery Water Management Authority order allocating 4.536 TMC is very less," the release added.Tamil Nadu has alleged that Karnataka has "failed" to release its due share and maintained that the state should receive 26.954 TMC.The Supreme Court will now hear the Tamil Nadu government's plea seeking immediate directions to Karnataka over the release of the Cauvery water.ALSO READ | Water released from KRS? North Korean leader Kim Jong Un reaffirmed the deepening of ties with Russia in a message to President Vladimir Putin as Pyongyang marked the anniversary of independence from Japan's colonial rule, KCNA state news agency said on Sunday.
Kim was replying to a message of congratulations from Putin marking Saturday's 81st anniversary of Tokyo's surrender in World War Two. The Russian leader said the bond was forged as Soviet soldiers fought against Japan and that cooperation would continue "in all the sectors."
The North Korean leader expressed hope for the future of ties that had "carried forward the history of common struggle for justice and precious traditions of friendship."
Pyongyang and Moscow have grown closer since the reclusive state began deploying troops and weapons to support Russia's war against Ukraine in what has been Pyongyang's most significant involvement in a war since the 1950s.
The Russian ship Pallada arrived at Wonsan port for a goodwill visit on Saturday tied to the liberation anniversary, and was greeted by North Korean provincial officials and Russian embassy staff, KCNA said.
Also on Saturday, South Korean President Lee Jae Myung called for talks with the rival North aimed at peaceful coexistence, telling Seoul's Liberation Day ceremony that the two Koreas need safeguards to prevent conflict and should work to replace their armistice with a "peace regime."
Lee urged dialogue to formally end the 1950-1953 Korean War, which ended in a ceasefire but no peace treaty, and said the talks could explore ways to curb Pyongyang's nuclear programme.
Pyongyang has rejected Lee's overtures and criticized U.S.-South Korean military exercises as provocations.
On Thursday, Putin drew Tokyo's condemnation with a visit to an island off Hokkaido, claimed by Japan, that Moscow seized in the days after Japan's 1945 surrender.

Bus crash in Hungary kills at least 12
August 16, 2026
At least 12 people have died after a Polish coach crashed into a ditch and overturned in eastern Hungary, police said on Sunday.
According to emergency services, 47 people were injured in the incident, 10 seriously.
What do we know about the accident?
The accident occurred on the M3 motorway near Mezokeresztes, around 140 kilometers (87 miles) east of Budapest, according to police in the district capital, Miskolc.
Police said they believe the driver fell asleep at the wheel during the overnight journey into Sunday. He was subsequently arrested.
Poland's PAP news agency reported that the bus had been carrying a group of pilgrims from Podkarpackie province in the far southeast of Poland.
The group, said to number 59 people, including two drivers, had been returning from Bosnia-Herzegovina, PAP said.
Fourteen ambulances were deployed to the scene of the crash, reports said.
Hungary's National Directorate for Disaster Management said that several of the passengers had been trapped under the vehicle when it overturned.
Condolences from Hungary, Poland
Hungarian Prime Minister Peter Magyar has voiced his condolences to the families of the crash victims in a Facebook message and thanked emergency and rescue services.
Polish President Karol Nawrocki said he was deeply shaken. "In the face of this unimaginable tragedy, which affects us all, my thoughts and prayers go out to the families and loved ones of the victims," the 43-year-old wrote on X.

The death toll from the earthquake in Indonesia has risen to 51
Kyiv • UNN
On Indonesia’s Flores Island, 51 people were killed and another 36 seriously injured as a result of a magnitude 7.7 earthquake. About 5,000 people have been evacuated, and 341 aftershocks have been recorded.
The death toll from the magnitude 7.7 earthquake on Indonesia’s Flores Island has risen to 51. This was reported by Reuters, according to UNN.
Details
About 5,000 people were evacuated after a magnitude 7.7 earthquake struck eastern Indonesia, killing at least 51 people, blocking roads and triggering landslides, authorities said on Sunday
It was also reported that 36 people suffered serious injuries as a result of the earthquake, which struck the province of East Nusa Tenggara on Saturday morning, while 77 sustained minor injuries.
The earthquake, which was followed by around 341 aftershocks, is the deadliest in the Southeast Asian country since the 2022 earthquake that claimed the lives of hundreds of people in West Java.
More than 3,300 people in the Sikka region evacuated on their own or were staying at a sports arena, the disaster management agency BNPB reported.
Some Sikka residents became stranded near destroyed homes under an improvised tarpaulin tent, while others were receiving treatment in a tent near a hospital in the port city of Maumere.

Earlier, the university said that police were looking for multiple suspects, the police, however, have not provided any information regarding this claim, only saying that they did not believe there was an immediate threat to the campus community, and that the campus lockdown had been lifted.
"We recognize the concern this incident has caused among our students, parents, alumni, friends, and the broader VSU community," the university's statement said. "The safety and well-being of our students remain our highest priority."
Arthur Fridrich, former university director who lives near the campus said that a shooting like this just as students return for classes is heartbreaking for the community, he continued:
"To start a new year with this event is very tragic. It casts a shadow in the minds of all students, and for some it will be difficult to rid their minds of this term," Fridrich said. "For those that were shot, my heart bleeds. I hope that they all mend and somehow do not let this event define their lives."

Indoor ‘feels-like’ heat soars to 52 degrees in Hong Kong subdivided homes: study
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-16
09:41:29 UTC
18:41:29 KST

Subdivided flat residents suffering in heat that feels like 52 degrees: study
Survey of 86 households across nine districts finds 80 per cent of people living in such homes reported dizziness and headaches
Indoor heat levels in Hong Kong’s subdivided flats and rooftop huts felt like a blistering 52.21 degrees Celsius (126 Fahrenheit) this summer, with 80 per cent of homemakers living in those homes reporting dizziness and headaches, according to a survey released on Sunday.
The study, conducted by CarbonCare InnoLab and the Concerning Subdivided Units Alliance, surveyed 86 households across nine districts from June 22 to July 12, with 78 living in subdivided flats or rooftop huts, among other inadequate housing units.
It measured “apparent temperatures” – referring to how hot people actually feel, taking humidity into account – which averaged 35.58 degrees in the daytime, with the highest of 52.21 degrees recorded in a subdivided flat, the survey found.
Average temperatures reached 29.93 degrees during the day and 29.42 degrees at night, both exceeding the Hong Kong Observatory’s threshold of 28 degrees for a “hot night”.
According to the Observatory, the monthly mean temperature for July, recorded at its headquarters in Tsim Sha Tsui, was 28.7 degrees. The heat persisted on Sunday, with the highest temperature reaching 34 degrees.
Homemakers, who made up 48 per cent of the households surveyed, were the most affected group, with about 83 per cent saying they often or always felt fatigued.

====================================================================================================

A positive new report raises the question: was Reeves undermined by dodgy data? | Heather Stewart
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-16
09:30:05 UTC
18:30:05 KST

The keen new chancellor, John Healey, responded to last week’s better-than-expected economic news by claiming the government was “bringing hope back”. Growth did not plunge as feared after Donald Trump unleashed war on Iran – with GDP expanding at a pretty decent 0.4% in the second quarter.
But what if we should have held on to a bit more hope all along? A new assessment of the UK’s recent productivity suggests this critical measure of the country’s economic strength may have been systematically underestimated.
Instead of stagnation, it points to a “meaningful pickup” in productivity since mid-2024, with annual growth of about 1.6% – up from an average of 0.3% in the previous decade.
This has very much not been the prevailing narrative since Labour came to power. Indeed, Rachel Reeves spent months last year scrambling to respond to a downgrade in productivity projections from the Office for Budget Responsibility (OBR) – from 1.3% annual growth to 1% – with a knock-on effect for the public finances.
Other things being equal, weaker productivity means weaker growth, which broadly translates to lower tax revenues and a bigger public deficit.
The OBR rethink didn’t reflect anything Labour had done, resulting instead from the long-term failure of productivity growth to bounce back after the 2008 global financial crisis. And part of the reason it became so pivotal was because Reeves had left herself so little room for manoeuvre.
But the productivity downgrade contributed to the gloomy sense that Labour was overseeing an economy beset by intractable long-term challenges. And it increased the size of the tax grab Reeves needed to make at last year’s budget to rebuild the headroom against her fiscal rules and pay for Labour’s welfare U-turn.
The new estimates, from the Centre for Economic Performance at the London School of Economics (LSE), where former Reeves advisers John Van Reenen and Anna Valero have now returned to their desks, paint a markedly different picture.
Productivity is defined as how much output each worker produces, but the UK has been botching the job of sizing up the workforce now for several years. The beleaguered Office for National Statistics (ONS) withdrew the status of accredited official statistic from its labour force survey (LFS) in 2024 as it struggled with plunging response rates from consumers.
Instead of using the LFS, which the OBR has to rely on, the LSE co-authors, including Van Reenen and Valero, together with Niki Barbas, use estimates made by the Resolution Foundation thinktank.
Resolution’s approach relies on an alternative dataset published by the ONS, based on what companies tell the tax authorities through the PAYE system (augmented with other sources to account for the self-employed).
The differences are wide. While the LFS records a 377,000 increase in the number of employees since mid-2024, the tax-based measure shows a decline of 133,000.
Of course, depending on what’s happened to those missing workers – retirement, unemployment, sickness, childcare – this may be a different cause for concern. Reeves has been accused of depressing hiring by piling costs on to employers.
But using the smaller estimate for the number of employees suggests that far from flatlining, productivity has jumped. That raises the intriguing possibility that, with better data, the OBR downgrade, and the massive headache it created for the then chancellor, could have been avoided.
Van Reenen says that “the best current guess does suggest we are getting more out of our workers than we used to”.
He dismisses the idea that what has happened is just layoffs among low-skilled workers, pushing up average productivity. “I don’t think that’s the main story: a chunk of this appears to be real.”
It’s too early to say what may be driving an uplift in productivity, let alone whether it will be sustained – but one hypothesis is that AI is starting to bear fruit in some sectors.
“It’s certainly a possibility that we are seeing the first signs of that starting to happen,” Van Reenen says.
Not surprisingly, he points to his former boss Reeves’s policies – including a significant increase in public investment and the stripping back of planning rules – as reasons to hope the improvement could continue.
The latest official GDP figures showed business investment – widely seen as one determinant of productivity – rising strongly, though experts were quick to caution that it could be reversed as high energy prices take their toll.
Whatever the future brings, the wide discrepancy with the official figures underlines how urgent a priority it should have been to fix the gaping holes in the UK’s jobs data earlier, and more effectively.
The poorly resourced ONS has been doggedly developing a new, online version of the LFS. Instead of the cumbersome 40-45 minute phone call needed to complete the existing questionnaire, it takes about 15 minutes.
In an update last week, the ONS acknowledged that the refreshed survey design appeared to be turning up slightly different results – including, for example, lower levels of long-term sickness. It also confirmed that it would be November next year at the earliest before it could switch over to the new version.
The UK has had no national statistician, the head of the ONS, for more than a year since Ian Diamond resigned in May 2025. The vacancy hardly speaks of burning urgency in Whitehall.
Some of Labour’s worst domestic struggles over the past two years, from winter fuel to the welfare row, were self-inflicted. But as Reeves returns to the backbenches this autumn, she could be excused for feeling her challenges at No 11 were exacerbated by dodgy data.

On 14 August 2026, Polish broadcaster RMF FM identified American-Ukrainian rapper and video blogger Kyivstoner as the previously unnamed target of an alleged Russian-directed assassination plot in Warsaw. The case comes as European authorities investigate suspected Russian attacks and sabotage across the continent.
The alleged plot against Kyivstoner comes amid attacks on Kremlin critics abroad, including the fatal shooting of a Russian opposition artist in Poland in June.
Polish authorities disclosed the Kyivstoner's case on 13 August but withheld the target’s identity. RMF’s identification points to a possible motive, though it relies on unverified allegations from the FSB, Russia's domestic security agency that Kyivstoner of managed drone deliveries intended for attacks near Moscow.
Who is Kyivstoner?
Kyivstoner was born Albert Vasiliev and uses the name Slevin Dadyan on his US passport. He gained attention through humorous videos and the Ukrainian group Hryby before releasing solo tracks, including “Leto” (Summer) and “Zvuk” (Sound).
In a 2025 interview, Vasiliev voiced support for Ukrainians and opposition to Russian occupation, saying Russian ruler Vladimir Putin made him angry and that he wanted civilians and soldiers to stop dying.
In July 2026, Russia’s FSB accused Kyivstoner of overseeing logistics for a foiled drone attack on a defense enterprise near Moscow.
The agency alleged that 35 drones assembled in Kyiv were concealed in a shipment of ceramic tiles and smuggled into Russia through Slovakia, Poland, and Belarus. Russian authorities also added Vasiliev to a register of people they label as involved in extremist or terrorist activity.
Vasiliev responded on Instagram by mocking Russia's allegation, saying he had been relaxing and playing video games rather than organizing an attack.
Russian authorities also accuse him of cooperating with Ukrainian intelligence. He denies the accusations, and RMF offered no independent evidence to substantiate them.
Suspect detained before alleged attack
Prime Minister Donald Tusk said Polish services detained the Russian suspect on 7 August, stopping the alleged attack “at the last minute.” US services assisted the operation. A Polish court remanded the man in custody for three months.
The journalists described the Russian citizen as a native of Donbas in eastern Ukraine. Tusk said the target, who holds Ukrainian and US passports, was “inconvenient to the Putin regime.”
The prime minister called it the first Russian-ordered attempt of its kind against a US citizen in another NATO country.
Killings and disrupted plots across Europe
Throughout Europe, Russia has tried to hunt down and kill anti-Kremlin critics and supporters of Ukraine. In June, Russian opposition artist Robert Kuzovkov, known as Semyon Skrepetsky, was shot dead in eastern Poland. US and German services also reportedly foiled a Russian plot against Rheinmetall CEO Armin Papperger in 2024. German intelligence later treated the surveillance of Bavarian drone manufacturer Donaustahl’s CEO as a suspected planned assassination.

‘You fall in love with the sky instantly’: Personnel of Lida-based air base share their stories
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-16
09:25:00 UTC
18:25:00 KST

“Take off, fight, win” is the motto of the Lida-based 116th Guards Radom Red Banner Assault Air Base, whose history began in September 1941 in Moscow Oblast. In October 1943, the pilots were awarded the Red Banner. They liberated Belarus, Poland, and East Prussia. In 1983-1984, the personnel took part in combat operations in Afghanistan. Eighty-five years later, the pilots continue the combat traditions established by their predecessors. BelTA’s correspondents visited the air base and spoke with the servicemen.
At the 116th Air Base, everyone serves with purpose. Behind the controls of Yak-130s, L-39s, and Su-25s are Belarusians who have found their calling -defending the skies of their homeland. One of them is the Deputy Commander of the Combat Training Aviation Squadron for Ideological Work, Guards Major Bronislav Zharsky. Behind him are 5 years of study at the Military Academy, 11 years of officer service, and over a thousand flight hours.
Bronislav Zharsky is a 1st-class military pilot. He chose his path after studying at the Minsk Suvorov Military School. However, according to him, all dreams come from childhood.
“I think every boy, and probably every girl too, dreams in childhood of going to space; many dream of becoming cosmonauts. Children also have dreams of flying. You'd think that when you get up that high, it must feel pretty special. I was that kind of child too. When I was little, I would stand on a chair, stretch my arms out to the sides, and ask my parents to catch me. That’s how I imagined flying. I approached these dreams more consciously toward the end of military school. The understanding of who I wanted to be came at 16 or 17,” Bronislav Zharsky said. “My father immediately supported my choice. He himself is a serviceman. Maybe he would have preferred me to choose a different progression, but still. My mother was, of course, worried.”
Like all pilots, Bronislav Zharsky remembers his first flight: “No one will ever forget their first solo flight - those feelings, those emotions when you take to the sky. You have reached your dream; in that moment comes the realization that there is no turning back. From the very first seconds, you fall in love with the freedom, the sky, and the flying profession.”
Difficulties in service can only come from a lack of knowledge, the pilot believes. “The more you study, the more you fly, the greater your flying skills become. And each subsequent flight becomes a little simpler, a little easier. But you need to understand that no flight is like the previous one. Every time you take to the sky, there are new tasks and nuances. I would say that our work is not difficult, but responsible, because you know perfectly well that your flight, the completion of your mission, affects not only your personal result but that of the entire military unit. Therefore, every time you take off in an aircraft, you try to leave all your worries, troubles, and problems on the ground, so that you can fly with a clear mind, thinking of nothing, so that nothing gets in the way,” Bronislav Zharsky noted. 
Over the years of service, the pilot has identified three key elements important in his work: knowledge, which enables you to act correctly and coolly in any situation; a responsible attitude to the task; and calmness - all emotions must remain outside the cockpit. “Our pilots are all friendly, the instructors are good, and so are the commanders. Everyone always tries to be accommodating, always helps and supports. If needed, they will teach, show, or tell you where to read up or watch,” Bronislav Zharsky added. 
An important aspect for every serviceman, including pilots, is family support. “I would like to spend more time with my family, but such is our work: gritting your teeth, gathering all your strength and will and only forward. My wife is proud that I am a pilot. She worries, of course, but tries not to show her emotions. The children know what their dad does for a living. I know they are also proud of me,” the deputy commander said. 
For pilot Dmitry, the path to aviation began with advice from his platoon commander at the Suvorov Military School. “He was a paratrooper. He suggested I try my hand at aviation, assuming I would like it. He said that my head worked in the right direction, my hands could handle things, and I would manage. I went to study, but I didn't know if it would work out or not. In the end, most of my life has been in the military. There was nothing difficult in my studies; it was interesting, so the knowledge stuck, settled in, and everything went its own way, calmly and smoothly. Who in childhood doesn't dream of something distant and unattainable? But I never seriously thought that I could be connected with the sky,” he said. 
After nine years of service and over 800 flight hours, Dmitry still feels a slight excitement every time in anticipation of a flight. “But when you sit in the aircraft, the work begins. You immediately forget that you were a little nervous, and you just do your job. When you take to the sky, you get incredible pleasure. This is what you love, and what you have grown accustomed to.” 
“We have people of different temperaments, different mindsets, and different characters. But the main thing in our line of work is to have a cool head and a warm heart, so as to stay in this profession and love it. Everything else is skills and abilities,” he added.
For every pilot, his aircraft is a faithful comrade, the condition of which depends on a great many people who treat the winged machines with no less reverence. The head of the aircraft engine maintenance and repair group, Guards Major Dmitry Shchedov, is one of those responsible for the heart of the aircraft - its engine. He began his service at the 116th Air Base in 2015 as a senior aircraft technician. “I served for four years. Then I was offered a position in the technical-operational unit, in the engine group. I naturally agreed. The operations here are very responsible; attentiveness and control determine everything. After some time, I became the head of the engine group. I really enjoyed engine maintenance; testing the power plants is fascinating. The sound of an engine is truly like the beating of a human heart. But, for example, a person can complain about something, whereas machinery cannot, so you have to search for the issue. Therefore, the most important things in our work are attentiveness and timely maintenance,” Dmitry Shchedov said.
The man added that in their line of work, one cannot do without a love for machinery. “I’ve had that since childhood. I always knew I would choose a technical specialty. I learned about the Military Academy when I was faced with the choice of going into air defense or the aviation faculty. For some reason, I was more drawn to aviation, and from there everything started rolling,” Dmitry Shchedov said. “There was a fellow countryman of mine on the admissions committee (I'm originally from Vitebsk) and he asked what I liked more. I shared that I was more interested in turning wrenches. So he pointed me in that direction.”
After 11 years of service, Dmitry Shchedov has not lost his love for machinery: “I like planes, I like how they fly, how they sound. It’s so beautiful and unusual. But in our profession, there are no white-handed workers, regardless of rank, sometimes you have to roll up your sleeves and get to work.”
Every person serving at the Lida-based 116th Assault Air Base is a backbone and foundation of a large system. The coordinated work of all servicemen is the key to the safe operation of aviation equipment. The work of technical specialists guarantees that every flight goes without a hitch, and the skill of the pilots, whose professionalism is honed over years, allows them to confidently handle the most complex tasks. Today, on their professional holiday, special attention is given to the servicemen of the Air Force. “Our grandfathers and fathers passed the banner of the Air Force into our hands. They established the traditions. Today, we confidently hold this banner in our hands and build upon those traditions. We are proud of the feats accomplished by our grandfathers during the Great Patriotic War. Most importantly, today we are raising the youth who will carry this banner forward in the future. We thank all those who are with us in the sky, and we thank everyone who waits for us on the ground,” said the acting commander of the 116th Assault Air Base, Guards Colonel Dmitry Yermakov. 
Every military unit is an integral link in the national security system. The country’s defense capability depends on their coordinated work. Clear coordination, discipline, and readiness for immediate response in each unit form a reliable shield that protects the country from threats. Pilots stand at a special frontier of defense. Their skill and composure make it possible to control the airspace and respond swiftly to any challenges. Every flight is not only a demonstration of technical power but also a guarantee that the skies over Belarus remain under reliable protection.
Katerina Loiko 
                
                
            At the 116th Air Base, everyone serves with purpose. Behind the controls of Yak-130s, L-39s, and Su-25s are Belarusians who have found their calling -defending the skies of their homeland. One of them is the Deputy Commander of the Combat Training Aviation Squadron for Ideological Work, Guards Major Bronislav Zharsky. Behind him are 5 years of study at the Military Academy, 11 years of officer service, and over a thousand flight hours.
Bronislav Zharsky is a 1st-class military pilot. He chose his path after studying at the Minsk Suvorov Military School. However, according to him, all dreams come from childhood.
“I think every boy, and probably every girl too, dreams in childhood of going to space; many dream of becoming cosmonauts. Children also have dreams of flying. You'd think that when you get up that high, it must feel pretty special. I was that kind of child too. When I was little, I would stand on a chair, stretch my arms out to the sides, and ask my parents to catch me. That’s how I imagined flying. Ukraine Wipes Out 75 Russian Drones Over Sumy, Including Rare $100,000 Knyaz Veschyi Oleg
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-16
09:23:01 UTC
18:23:01 KST

- Category
- War in Ukraine
Ukraine Wipes Out 75 Russian Drones Over Sumy, Including Rare $100,000 Knyaz Veschyi Oleg
Ukrainian air-defense drone operators have destroyed 75 Russian aerial targets over Sumy region since the beginning of August, including 53 Molniya-2 strike drones and a rare Knyaz Veschyi Oleg reconnaissance UAV valued at around $100,000.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
Ukraine’s 47th Separate Mechanized Brigade “Magura” reported on August 15 that its Sky Wars unit had intercepted 53 Molniya-2 drones, six ZALA Lancet loitering munitions, six FPV drones, three ZALA reconnaissance UAVs, three Gerbera drones, two drones identified as “Bombers,” one Knyaz Veschyi Oleg and one Mavic quadcopter.
Molniya-2s accounted for more than two-thirds of the total. The fixed-wing Russian FPV drone is designed as a relatively inexpensive platform for tactical strikes and reconnaissance.
Serhii Beskrestnov, an adviser to the President of Ukraine on defense technology development, estimated its cost at about $1,600, putting the value of the 53 destroyed aircraft at roughly $84,800.
The six Lancets represent a significantly more expensive part of the losses. Developed by ZALA Aero, the Lancet family consists of loitering munitions used to locate and strike battlefield targets.
Beskrestnov estimated the newer X-52 at around $40,000 and the larger X-51 at about $68,000. Since the brigade did not specify the variants, the six destroyed Lancets could be worth approximately $240,000 to $408,000.
Among the rarest targets was the Knyaz Veschyi Oleg, a Russian tactical reconnaissance UAV developed by the Ushkuynik research and production center.
Ukraine’s Defense Intelligence lists it as having a 2.8-meter wingspan, endurance of up to 3.5 hours, an operational radius of around 45 kilometers and a maximum speed of 130 km/h. Ukrainian military units have previously valued the drone at approximately $100,000.
Sky Wars also destroyed three Gerbera drones. The Russian UAV is built largely from inexpensive materials and is commonly used as a decoy resembling Shahed-type attack drones, although reconnaissance and armed variants also exist.
Ukrainian estimates have placed its production cost at around $10,000 per aircraft, giving the three destroyed Gerberas an estimated value of about $30,000.
The brigade did not specify the models of the three ZALA reconnaissance UAVs, six FPVs, two “Bombers,” or the Mavic, making their value difficult to determine reliably.
Based only on the 53 Molniya-2s, six Lancets, three Gerberas and the Knyaz Veschyi Oleg, the 63 identifiable drones had an estimated combined value of approximately $454,800 to $622,800. The real total for all 75 destroyed aircraft would therefore be higher.
Ukraine has also been pushing interceptor drones to greater altitudes. On August 2, border guards using a STING FPV interceptor destroyed a Russian ZALA Z-20 reconnaissance UAV at 6,858 meters over Chernihiv region, setting what Ukrainian authorities described as a world record for drone-on-drone interception.

Russian Drone Hunts Combine in Ukrainian Wheat Field, Killing Farmer During Harvest
A Russian drone struck agricultural machinery harvesting a field in Ukraine’s Zaporizhzhia region on August 15, killing a 32-year-old man and injuring another, Ukrainian emergency officials reported.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
Ukraine’s State Emergency Service (SES) said the drone targeted farm equipment operating during the harvest in the Zaporizhzhia region. The injured man received medical assistance following the attack.
The strike set fire to a combine harvester, a passenger vehicle, and wheat growing in the field. Emergency crews extinguished the resulting blaze, according to the SES.
Photos released by emergency officials showed the damaged agricultural machinery and burned sections of the field following the strike.
The latest attack follows another deadly Russian strike in Zaporizhzhia earlier this week. On August 11, a Russian ballistic missile hit a Metinvest industrial site, killing seven employees and injuring 21 others. The strike severely damaged the facility and forced the primary metallurgical plant to suspend operations, according to Metinvest.

Switzerland allocates CHF600,000 to restore Kyiv monastery
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

Switzerland allocates CHF600,000 to restore Kyiv monastery
Switzerland will provide CHF600,000 ($737,000) to help secure and restore the Kyiv-Pechersk Lavra, a historic 11th-century UNESCO World Heritage Site in Kyiv, Ukraine, damaged in a recent Russian air strike.
The funding was announced in Kyiv on Saturday by Jacques Gerber, the Swiss government’s delegate for Ukraine, during events marking the monastic complex’s 975th anniversary. The complex, also known as the Monastery of the Caves, is one of Ukraine’s most important religious and cultural landmarks.
The Dormition Cathedral and several historic buildings were badly damaged in a Russian attack on June 15. The same day, Swiss President Guy Parmelin and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky discussed possible Swiss support for assessing the damage during talks in Geneva.
More
Swiss aid to Ukraine amounts to more than CHF6 billion
Restoration work will be carried out by UNESCO in cooperation with the Ukrainian authorities. Gerber said cultural heritage plays a vital role in preserving the country’s identity and social cohesion.
The contribution is part of Switzerland’s Ukraine programme, which has a budget of CHF1.5 billion for 2025-2028.

09:17:22 UTC
18:17:22 KST

Israel Police on Sunday requested the public's help in locating a 16-year-old from Acre who has been missing since late July, after being granted permission by the family to publicize details of the case.
Karim Abdel Kader was last seen on July 20 after leaving his school in I'billin, located in northern Israel near Shefar'am.
Kader has black hair, dark skin, and was last seen wearing a black shirt and matching pants. Police stated that he does not have a phone on him.
Police have asked anyone with information on his whereabouts to either report it to the police hotline (100) or to the Acre Police Station over the phone at 04-987-6808.
The announcement of Kader's disappearance comes days after a separate missing persons case that gripped Israel was solved.
Police locate Mali, Liel Yahalomi
On Friday, police announced that Israeli mother Mali Yahalomi and her daughter, Liel, had been found alive on an intercity bus in Buenos Aires, Argentina.
The two left Israel for Prague, continued to Vienna, apparently traveled through Frankfurt, before eventually reaching Buenos Aires. They had been reported missing nearly a week ago after failing to check in with family members after a Shabbos spent in Vienna.
Authorities are continuing to investigate the circumstances of the trip, including why the two women traveled from Europe to Argentina and did not make contact while police were trying to locate them.
Police suspect the two recorded videos for their family in Vienna but sent them after leaving the country, creating the impression they were still there, Ynet reported. The investigation also reportedly found that their travel was connected to personal financial circumstances.
