The best person for the role - comment
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-16
07:05:35 UTC
16:05:35 KST

Justice Minister Yariv Levin has declared that if the Likud wins the Knesset elections, he will ask to continue in his post so that he can finally implement his judicial reform policy.
What needs reform even more is the size of the government. Admittedly, every party in a government coalition should be entitled to one minister, but regardless of the size of the party whose leader is the prime minister, no party, other than the ruling party, should have more than one minister in the government. The ruling party can have an extra minister in addition to the prime minister.
In delegating ministerial portfolios, the prime minister should forget about jobs for the boys and appoint the most suitable people from those who received the most votes in the primaries held by their respective political parties.
There were 12 ministers in the first government of Israel. The present government started with 30 ministers but now has 24. It’s not the largest government. There were two governments with 36 ministers. Naftali Bennett led Benjamin Netanyahu the other.
For political convenience, new portfolios are created, and some old portfolios are canceled or renamed.
In addition to the prime minister, ministries in the present government include: agriculture and food security; aliyah and integration; communications; construction and housing; culture and sports; defense; economy and industry; education; energy and infrastructure; environmental protection; finance; foreign affairs; health; heritage; innovation, science, and technology; interior; justice; national security; Negev, Galilee, and national resilience; religious services; social equality and the advancement of the status of women; tourism: transportation and road safety; and welfare and social affairs. In addition, numerous national authorities and other national bodies are engaged in formulating and determining policy.
By contrast, portfolios in Israel’s first government included agriculture, rationing and supply; education and culture; foreign affairs; finance, trade and industry; health; immigration and internal affairs; justice; labor and social security; police; religions and war victims; transportation; and welfare.
Issues further arise with the handling of these core ministries, such as education.
To the early governments of Israel, education was of primary importance after defense and diplomacy. In fact, a law on compulsory education was passed during the period of the first government.
But interest in education appears to be waning as teachers are made to work harder for less money and fewer vacation days.
There is almost always friction between official representatives of teachers’ unions and the Education Ministry, with threats and fears that some schools will not open at the beginning of September. This year is no different, but the situation is exacerbated by reports that teaching is no longer a desirable profession, and that there has been a sharp drop in the number of people opting for a career in education.
Education Minister Yoav Kisch has been quoted as saying that he loves the ministry and hopes to continue as minister if Likud wins the Knesset election.
But Kisch is not popular with teachers or their unions. If his wish comes true, more teachers will leave the profession. There is already an acute shortage of teachers. If their ranks continue to be depleted, what hope is there for Israel’s future?
Needed: An Israeli ministry for civil rights
In addition, though top-heavy with ministerial portfolios, some of which could either be merged or eliminated, Israel’s government desperately needs a ministry or authority for national priorities and the implementation of civil rights.
Israel’s founding fathers, namely the signatories to the Declaration of Independence, though coming from vastly different ideologies, agreed that “the State of Israel will ensure complete equality of social and political rights to all citizens, irrespective of religion, race or sex. It will guarantee freedom of religion, conscience, language, education and culture. It will safeguard the Holy Places of all religions…..”
There’s a missing word – “residents.” It’s a known fact that certain residents of Israel who wish to become citizens have had their applications denied year after year. Some who are non-Jewish, but were married to Israeli Jews and have Israeli-born children, were deported after divorce or widowhood.
Some Arabs whose families have lived in this country for generations are also denied citizenship and most of the civil rights that go with it.
How can we ever make peace with the Palestinians while continuing to discriminate against Arabs in our midst?
Some of the Arabs living in Israel are married to Arabs living in Gaza. Before October 7, the Gazan spouse used to come to Israel every few weeks for two or three days. This is no longer permitted, and families rely on social media platforms to stay connected. If the Gazan spouse had been coming to Israel for years and never violated any Israeli laws, is it not a violation of the civil rights of the partner living in Israel to keep the two of them apart?
When Soviet authorities imprisoned Natan Sharansky and kept him apart from his wife Avital for 12 years until they were reunited with the help of US president Ronald Reagan, US diplomacy, and a prisoner exchange, the mobilization of world Jewry for the whole period in which Sharansky was incarcerated kept the issue burning.
Gazan spouses barred from Israel don’t have that kind of support, though their plight is occasionally mentioned in left-wing publications and on social media.
Of course they cannot be compared with Sharansky, who was a dissident dedicated to exposing Soviet tyranny and facilitating the emigration of Soviet Jews. But the bottom line in both cases is the break-up of family.
Family break-ups among Israeli families have also occurred because the husband, a reservist, spent too long away from home while serving in the army and was not adequately compensated for the loss of income.
There has to be a ministry other than social welfare that concerns itself with humane and human rights issues.

Haymanot Kasau's parents demand equal resources after missing mother, daughter found in one week
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-16
07:05:32 UTC
16:05:32 KST

The family of Haymanot Kasau, who disappeared in Safed at age nine in 2024 and has been missing for more than 900 days, has renewed their push for a more extensive search. The move follows the discovery of Mali and Liel Yahalomi in Argentina only about a week after they disappeared in Vienna and following an extensive search operation by the Israel Police in Israel and abroad.
Haymanot’s family is demanding that the same capabilities and resources used in the search for Mali and Liel also be employed in the investigation into her disappearance and is calling for the case to be transferred to the Shin Bet (Israeli Security Agency).
A statement from the campaign headquarters seeking Haymanot’s return home said, “With the mother and daughter having been found and Israel Police succeeding in solving the investigation, its helplessness in investigating Haymanot’s abduction stands out even more, and therefore the family is demanding that the investigation be transferred to the Shin Bet.”
Haymanot’s parents, Benchi and Tesfaye Kasau, also responded to the discovery of the two women, saying that alongside their joy that the case ended safely, they could not help but compare the efforts invested in that search with the handling of their daughter’s case.
“After Shabbat ended, we received the happy news that Mali and Liel Yahalomi had been found safe and well. Once again, a happy ending, except it is not our happy ending. Our Haymanot has not been with us for 902 days. 902 days have passed since our little daughter was abducted.”
The parents added, “Haymanot was nine years old; she did not choose to disappear, she did not choose not to come home, and despite this, not everything possible has been done to find her. Israel Police, under the direction of Insp.-Gen. Danny Levy, used all of its capabilities to find Mali and Liel, but what have they done for our Haymanot? Lahav 433 has investigated half the world to find them, and they still don’t meet with us or update us properly.
“We are once again asking Israel Police to transfer the investigation into Haymanot’s abduction to the Shin Bet, and that Police Commissioner Insp.-Gen. Danny Levy and Lahav 433 head Commissioner Meni Binyamin, who have failed to find any lead in the investigation, transfer the case to the Shin Bet because our girl is still not here.”
In an appeal to the public, the parents said, “And to the dear people of Israel, whose citizens continue to show us the light amid all the darkness, and we understand that many of them, like us, have expressed their anger over the discrimination in the handling of the investigation into Haymanot’s abduction, thank you. Thank you very much, and please, stay with us; help us make our cry heard because, unfortunately, no one listens to us.”
Mother, daughter found in Argentina after planning disappearance
Mali and Liel Yahalomi captured the country’s imagination over the past week as the mystery surrounding their disappearance from the streets of Vienna unfolded. On Friday night, Israel Police announced that the two had been located on a bus in Argentina, safe and well. Police questioned them and released them after they said that they had left of their own free will. Police clarified that they had no suspicion of criminal activity and had not opened an investigation.
Details revealed after they were found indicated that the two had planned their disappearance in advance, but had not taken into account law enforcement authorities’ ability to trace digital footprints and piece together information collected in different countries.
“Israel Police, in cooperation with all security agencies and relevant authorities in Israel and abroad, operated in recent days in an extensive and focused effort to locate the missing women,” the police stated.
“At the direction of Police Commissioner Insp.-Gen. Danny Levy, the police, led by Lahav 433 and the Intelligence Division, operated command centers in Israel and abroad around the clock. According to the police, all necessary means and resources were allocated to the searches, hundreds of investigative actions were carried out, and cooperation took place with Europol and other police organizations around the world.”
A police source told Maariv, “From the outset, we said that there apparently was no criminal incident or terrorist incident here, and that the mother and daughter had most likely left the room [in Vienna] of their own free will. Representatives of the police Intelligence Division managed to track them down, and they were surprised when we reached them. After a brief questioning, and once we understood that there was no criminal or other motive, they were released. There is no suspicion that they committed an offense.”
Haymanot Kasau's family marks 900 days since disappearance
Haymanot Kasau disappeared from an absorption center in Safed more than 900 days ago and has not been found since. Her family said police still have no leads in the case and have long demanded Shin Bet involvement.
On Wednesday, family members, members of the campaign to bring Haymanot home, and activists demonstrated near the Shin Bet offices in Tel Aviv, calling on Shin Bet chief David Zini to make the agency’s intelligence capabilities available to the investigation.
During the protest, Haymanot’s father, Tesfaye Kasau, read a personal letter he had written to Zini in Amharic, after which its contents were also read in Hebrew. “Tomorrow we will mark 900 days that our daughter has not been home, and my heart is struggling to bear the pain, the worry, and the helplessness,” the father wrote.
The family argues that the investigation should also be transferred to the Shin Bet in light of the agency’s involvement in other areas, including the fight against organized crime and weapons trafficking in Arab society and the search for the child Yuval Kogan.
They say the agency’s resources and intelligence capabilities should also be made available in the effort to locate Haymanot.
In his letter, the father also raised a painful allegation regarding the way the case has been handled.
“I am doing everything in my power to stop myself from thinking that it has to do with color, but it is very difficult not to think about how things would have looked different if we looked different. If she were blonde, would her life matter more? If she were not a new immigrant, Ethiopian, would you already be helping us? Prove to us that this is not the case.”

Premier League fans’ previews: our club-by-club guide to 2026-27
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-16
07:00:20 UTC
16:00:20 KST

Arsenal
Having finally got the title monkey off our back, and with much of the competition in a state of flux, there’s plenty of optimism. Obviously the target is for Arteta to sustain the same appetite and intensity to mount a credible defence. The big questions are whether we can reproduce the same resilience at the back with Saliba on the long-term missing list, and will the introduction of Guimarães be the catalyst for the sort of midfield chemistry we’ll need to carve open opponents who plan to park the bus?
Key players/weak links On the evidence of our pre-season outings we urgently need the return of our remaining World Cup stars – Rice, Zubimendi and Saka should provide a renewed sense of purpose, both to counter any defensive fragility and to increase our goal threat. We’re all hoping for a breakthrough season for a beefed-up Max Dowman, and are anxious to discover if Tzolis is an upgrade on Trossard.
We still need to sign … Our friendly outings have shown the need for alternative attacking options, such as Atlético’s Julián Alvarez, and cover for Saliba – Quansah and Konsa are linked. But presumably any further arrivals will be dependent on some astute pruning of those who’ve failed to cut the mustard, such as Vieira and Nelson.
Our cult hero is … Benny Blanco’s off-the-ball shenanigans ensure that he’s enshrined as a firm terrace favourite, but it’s the demeanour of Declan Rice that will invariably set the tone for whether or not we’re destined for more success.
If we could sign two players from our past … Who wouldn’t want to add the artistry of Thierry Henry and Dennis Bergkamp to any team?
We will finish 1st. Top four: 1. Arsenal; 2. Chelsea; 3. Manchester City; 4. Liverpool. Bottom three: 18. Coventry; 19. Ipswich; 20. Hull. First manager sacked Sergej Jakirovic.
- 
  Bernard Azulay onlinegooner.com; @GoonerN5
Aston Villa
It would be daft to not be optimistic when each year under Emery we’ve created great memories, regardless of the previous summer’s transfer merry-go-round. Top six and a cup run of any flavour would count as a good season, and it may be that our best moments are back-end weighted as we integrate some exciting new talent. I understand that Manzambi is the best thing to come out of Switzerland since the cuckoo clock, and any 22-year-old with 187 senior appearances (Garnacho) must be all right. Perversely, the financial regulations that are holding us back should prevent too much moaning if we don’t get off to a flyer, and having a ground with only three sides might even help us make VP a fortress. In all, I’m fired up for the new season.
Key players/weak links The senior pros all need to keep drinking the Emery Kool Aid, but why wouldn’t they? Konsa remains a colossus and the purple prose around McGinn is fully deserved. If Kamara plays 40 senior games and not his usual 25 it will improve our finishing spot by two. Normally naming a young player to watch in these pages guarantees them a loan move to Lincoln, but Brian Madjo has looked immense up front in pre-season.
We still need to sign … Marcus Rashford.
Our cult hero is … McGinn must already have done enough to have a hospitality suite named after him. Another two years and it could be a stand. He will be aware that Emery doesn’t deal in sentimentality so I expect yet another year in which SJM pushes for player of the season while being a key figure in the dressing room.
If we could sign two players from our past … Dwight Yorke, from 1995-96 when he switched to an out-and-out striker. And Gareth Barry: the complete midfielder.
We will finish 6th. Top four: 1. Arsenal; 2. Manchester City; 3. Manchester United; 4. Chelsea. Bottom three: 18. Fulham; 19. Ipswich; 20. Hull. First manager sacked Roberto De Zerbi.
- 
  Jonathan Pritchard
Bournemouth
We’re so looking forward to this: our first ever season in a European club competition. It’s going to be monumental. And, with arguably our strongest ever squad to call on, we expect to be competitive in the Europa League too. We’re excited to see Marco Rose in charge and a continuation of the fast, attacking, no-fear brand of football that earned us our highest ever finish last season. In view of the extra games we have on the schedule, a mid-table Premier League finish would be very respectable, but winning a trophy feels weirdly achievable. Why not a European one?
Key players/weak links António Silva has big Senesi-sized shoes to fill at centre-half but we expect big things from him. We’re also looking forward to the impact that new striker Álvaro Rodríguez and the attacking right-back Juanlu will bring. Watch out too for a fully fit Ben Gannon-Doak – a breakthrough season beckons for him.
We still need to sign … Business is pretty much done. We’re in a good place, with maybe one or two to go out on loan deals towards the end of the window.
Our cult hero is … Long-serving veteran defender Adam Smith continues to perform at the highest level, an incredible 16 years after his debut for the club. He epitomises the journey we’ve been on and we love him for it.
If we could sign two players from our past … It would be hard to turn down a peak Nathan Aké or Callum Wilson, but then with the squad that we have now, I’m not convinced they would get into a starting 11. Perhaps, with Junior Kroupi out for a few months, there might be a place for a natural finisher like Jermain Defoe. Better still, prime Ted MacDougall would score hatfuls every week in this team.
We will finish 12th. Top four: 1. Manchester City; 2. Arsenal; 3. Liverpool; 4. Manchester United. Bottom three: 18. Hull; 19. Ipswich; 20. Leeds. First manager sacked Xabi Alonso.
- 
  Jeff Hayward Back of the Net, the AFC Bournemouth Fan’s Podcast
Brentford
I’m very optimistic. Twelve months ago we had Yoane Wissa refusing to train to force a move and the footballing world was convinced that our free-kick coach turned manager would get us relegated. Fast forward a year and things feel very different. We’ve had a proper pre-season, there’s a clear tactical approach and, importantly, we’ve signed players who can actually execute it. The target? Keep improving. If we can get a European spot this season, that would be another sign that we’re moving forward year-on-year. For a club like Brentford, that’s a pretty exciting prospect.
Key players/weak links There’s a lot of excitement around new signing Mamadou Sangaré – so much so that he’s already got his own song. Callum Wilson is a shrewd signing too, and, at this stage of his career, seems happy to sit on the bench and knock a few in when called upon. Our explosive front three of Ouattara, Thiago and Schade have now had time to gel, and should cause plenty of problems. As for youngsters, 11 players aged 21 or under are vying for a place in the final 25-man squad. 19-year-old striker – and rapper – Kaye Furo is highly rated, as is 20-year-old centre-back Jannik Schuster. It’s a good sign that we’re getting to the point where our youngsters aren’t just making up the numbers.
We still need to sign … If there’s one position we could strengthen, left-back would be a good option. El Hadji Malick Diouf from West Ham has been rumoured.
Our cult hero is … Michael Kayode. Cemented his status by singing his own terrace chant on camera: “He eats spaghetti, he drinks Moretti, he hates Queens Park Rangers.”
If we could sign two players from our past … We’re probably a bit too “nice”. Whenever we need a short injection of old-school fire, fight and chaos, Terry Evans from our 1992 Division One-winning side and Terry Hurlock from that incredible 80s “Kamara, Bowles, Hurlock” midfield would be great to call upon.
We will finish 6th. Top four: 1. Manchester City; 2. Arsenal; 3. Manchester United; 4. Bournemouth. Bottom three: 18. Fulham; 19. Ipswich; 20. Hull. First manager sacked I got it spot-on last season, predicting two consecutive Forest sackings. Surely Glasner isn’t next on the cards? OK, go on then …

  Billy Grant Beesotted podcast and blog; @Beesotted; @BillyTheBee99
Brighton
Having seen West Ham, Chelsea and even Crystal Palace go all the way in the Conference League, the main target is doing well in that and winning a first cup final since the 1910 Charity Shield. Am I optimistic about it happening? Not really. The competition looks tougher this year. Freiburg, Atalanta and Monaco all have proper European experience. Even the playoff round against Tromsø is a banana skin. I’m old enough to remember some pretty horrible trips to Carlisle when Brighton could never win north of Lake Windermere. Let alone inside the actual Arctic Circle.
Key players/weak links The key player will be whoever Fabian Hürzeler uses to fill the void left by selling Danny Welbeck: Georginio Rutter, Charalampos Kostoulas or Stefanos Tzimas. Not only did Welbeck score 13 goals last season, but most were vital equalisers or important winners worth 13 points. Allowing him to join Chelsea is a huge risk. If none of those younger alternatives who the club want playing more this season step up and replace Welbeck, there’s the weak link. And there are big question marks over all three.
We still need to sign … Danny Welbeck from Chelsea would be a good signing for his goals record and the experience he would bring to a young squad.
Our cult hero is … Rutter. Nothing says cult hero quite like having one Instagram account about your football career and another about the racehorses you own. With the racing one being more interesting.
If we could sign two players from our past … I’ll spare you another Welbeck answer and say Glenn Murray and Bobby Zamora instead. Hopefully, I’ll be able to revisit this on 3 June 2027 after we’ve just won the Conference League and Kostoulas has hit 46 goals in all competitions. Danny who?
We will finish 13th. Top four: 1. Arsenal; 2. Manchester United; 3. Manchester City; 4. Chelsea; Bottom three: 18. Sunderland; 19. Ipswich; 20. Hull. First manager sacked Oliver Glasner.

Chelsea
A new top manager, some decent new signings and a feelgood factor within the squad – it’s hard not to be optimistic. We’ve finally brought some experienced players who should complement our younger players and take them to the next level. With no Champions League football, the target has to be top four and a good run in the domestic cups.
Key players/weak links We’ve strengthened in most areas so it’s key that the new signings make a quick impact. The rest of the squad looks very balanced with strength in depth. At this stage of the window the main focus will be on trimming the squad to a manageable level.
Our cult hero is … In a team with few real characters I’m hoping some of the new signings will shake the squad up a bit. I’ve a feeling Pep Chavarría could quickly become a fan favourite with some dark arts. Cole Palmer will continue to entertain on and off the pitch with his great interviews.
If we could sign two players from our past … John Terry to marshal the defence and Frank Lampard to bang the goals in. Both players gave 100% every time they stepped on the pitch and were also fantastic motivators. Two absolute legends who would grace any team in any era.
We will finish Fourth. Top four: 1. Arsenal; 2. Manchester United; 3. Manchester City; 4. Chelsea. Bottom three: 18. Newcastle; 19. Ipswich; 20. Hull. First manager sacked Sergej Jakirovic.

Coventry
There’s no downside to choosing optimism, so yes, we’re optimistic. I don’t expect a top-half finish but I do enjoy how the club’s being run and believe in our ability to compete. Clearly the target is to survive, but within that, if we can showcase what’s good about us and provide a challenge, that would be a very acceptable return.
Key players/weak links The money we’ve spent is basically unfathomable, but my focus has been on those who were so critical to our promotion. Matt Grimes connects everyone in the team so we’re relying on him doing that again, else we’ll have to develop a completely new way to function. Signing keeper Carl Rushworth also gives assurance at the back that we hope will translate into points. There are questions about our strikers (which feels barmy for a team that scored 99 goals last season). It’s not complicated – we simply don’t know if Wright and Simms have what it takes to score at the highest level. Aside from signing Aurèle Amenda, we haven’t touched our defence either. It’s a bold strategy. Liam Kitching and Jay Dasilva have improved significantly, but it’s hard to ignore the notion that we’re relying on players like this finding another uptick. However, new signing Caleb Yirenkyi looks very special.
We still need to sign … We saw how vital Brian Brobbey was for Sunderland last season. A dynamic, high-status striker would go a long way towards calming the nerves about our forward line. Is Taiwo Awoniyi able to be that guy? Let’s hope so. The rumours about Fikayo Tomori are exciting. If we could bring him in, good lord.
Our cult hero is … While the returning Gus Hamer is clearly our cult hero, Milan van Ewijk is the joker of the team. You’ll find him front and centre of every celebration. But don’t let the daftness fool you; he’s a serious, serious player.
If we could sign two players from our past … The original version of James Maddison was unlike anything I’ve ever seen. His game has adapted with age, which is a shame, but I’d love some of that early ingenuity. I’d also welcome back Viktor Gyökeres. He functions far better when he believes he’s the star man. Come home Vik and bash your way to upwards of nine Premier League goals for Coventry.
We will finish 17th. Top four: 1. Manchester City, 2. Chelsea, 3. Arsenal, 4. Manchester United. Bottom three: 18. Ipswich, 19. Fulham, 20. Hull. First manager sacked Daniel Farke.

  Neil Allison @skybluesblog, Nii Lamptey Show Podcast
Crystal Palace
What are we expecting? Right now, it’s really difficult to say. The only key player to have exited (so far) is Maxence Lacroix, on whom we made a massive profit, but we still have to strengthen the squad so that it can cope with the rigours of going deep in the Europa League without risking our Premier League campaign – a lesson learned from last season. Lots of incoming deals seem close, but not yet over the line.
Key players/weak links Ismaïla Sarr and J-P Mateta will once again be essential, given the lack of goals in the rest of the squad. Adam Wharton will show how insane it was for Tuchel to leave him out of the World Cup, and Tyrick Mitchell will continue to excel on the left. Jaydee Canvot, still only 20, is destined to be a superb centre-back and should grow further in stature this season.
We still need to sign … There’s been some solid business already – US teenager Zavier Gozo and right-back Anan Khalaili look exciting prospects, and Evann Guessand is welcome back from Villa. But we still need a replacement for Lacroix, and strength in the middle – we had a £35m bid for Monaco’s Lamine Camara rejected. Plenty still to do. Meanwhile, the decision to swap Dwight McNeil for Brennan Johnson has split opinion: Johnson – all £35m of him – was only here a few months.
Our cult hero is … A few contenders. Mateta, obviously, chant-leader Dean Henderson and, potentially, our Brazilian attacker Matheus França. He’s not there yet, but he joined the club three years ago at 19 and has barely made an impact for various reasons. But he’s had a strong pre-season, including dancing goal celebrations – some Brazilian flair would go down very well at Selhurst.
If we could sign two players from our past … Michael Olise without a doubt; he was clearly a world-class player at Palace and has continued to progress spectacularly. And Matt Jansen, from the late 90s – a personal hero of mine; such incredible talent at such a young age and would shine in the modern era.
We will finish 14th. Top four: 1. Arsenal; 2. Manchester City; 3. Chelsea; 4. Tottenham. Bottom three: 18. Newcastle; 19. Ipswich; 20. Hull; First manager sacked Matthias Jaissle.
- 
  Chris Waters @Clapham_Grand
Everton
Despite the £327m the Friedkins have provided since the takeover, there are still doubts about the scale of their ambition. ‘Our children are less cognitively capable,’ says neuroscientist who wants to cut screen use in schools
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-16
07:00:20 UTC
16:00:20 KST

Jared Cooney Horvath is on a mission. In the wake of global campaigns for smartphone bans in schools and social media restrictions for under-16s, the neuroscientist wants to raise the alarm about educational technology in classrooms.
A former teacher, Horvath believes the use of screens and digital tools in schools is undermining how children learn and develop. “This might be one of the hardest truths our generation has to face,” he writes in his book, The Digital Delusion.
“Our children are less cognitively capable than we were at their age,” he says. “For nearly two centuries, the west experienced steady generational progress. Each new cohort of children grew up, on average, healthier, happier, and better educated than the last. Until now.”
Starting around the year 2000, something changed. “Across the west, IQ scores began to fall – even as time spent in school kept rising,” writes Horvath. Scores in international tests started to drop. Why? “The answer lies in the meteoric rise of educational technology.”
According to a recent Department for Education report, the UK educational technology – or edtech – market generated an annual turnover of about £6.5bn. In the US, Horvath says it is a $400bn (£295bn) mega-industry, woven into every aspect of schooling.
“We’ve been making some incredible strides on the screen-based childhood stuff which even two years ago, I did not think was going to happen as fast as it did,” he said. “But it’s not just about getting rid of screens for entertainment. It’s about reducing them as much as possible for academic learning as well if we want our kids to have deep transferrable knowledge in our heads.”
The uptake of laptops in schools – especially in the US where he lives – began in earnest in 2010-12, Horvath said. “It’s when Covid hit, that’s when every school had to pivot digital as a Band-Aid … rightly so. Better to have something than nothing.
“But when Covid finished you would assume they’d rip that Band-Aid off, but the vast majority of schools didn’t. They just stayed digital.” In the US 88% of school districts now had one-to-one computers, he said. In the UK, Covid had a similar impact.
Horvath has been studying how people learn for over 15 years and has concluded that “tech is not a very good tool for it”. He cites recent scores from the programme for international student assessment (Pisa) which takes place every three years and tracks the academic performance of 15-year-olds across dozens of countries.
In 2012, 2015 and 2018, Pisa asked students how much time they spent using digital devices during a typical school day. “The more time students spent on screens at school, the further their scores fell,” Horvath said. “On average, those who used computers for more than six hours per day scored 66 points lower than their peers who didn’t use them at all.”
Others working in the field are concerned about the risks of confusing correlation with causation. Rose Luckin is an emerita professor of learner-centred design at the UCL Knowledge Lab in London and a recognised expert on AI in education.
“[Horvath] does get certain things right,” Luckin said. “It’s true that a great deal of educational technology was sold on promises rather than proof. We did not have a huge amount of evidence. But that does not mean that all educational technology is problematic.
“In terms of that Pisa data, if you look at it on computer use and outcomes, actually moderate school device use is associated with better results than no school device use. It’s just that the heaviest daily use is the worst.”
Daisy Christodoulou, the director of education at No More Marking, an educational technology startup, agrees that society has been a “bit blase” about the impact of a lot of these new technologies.
“We are seeing across the board now a bit of a corrective, where people are realising that. But I would probably be a little bit more optimistic [than Horvath] about the potential for technology and AI in upper secondary,” she said. “Screens have not had as big an impact in classrooms in England as in the US. But I feel like there’s enough here that we should be thinking about it. I think it’s a bit blase to go, ‘nothing to see here’, move on please’.”
Dylan Wiliam, an emeritus professor of educational assessment at the UCL Institute of Education, said: “Technology may well be harming student achievement but the correlational studies that we currently have cannot support such causal claims.
“And there are many well-designed studies that show that technology can have a positive impact on student achievement. So the question, ‘Does edtech have a negative impact on learning?’ does not have a simple yes/no answer: sometimes it does, and sometimes it doesn’t.
“The question we need to be asking is, ‘when does edtech help learning?’ And the answer is, ‘it’s complicated’.”

AI cheating, leaked papers and marking errors: how exam protests went global
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-16
07:00:19 UTC
16:00:19 KST

Families with teenagers in education know the private, hidden pain of exam season. But this year, what might have been a summer of quiet family anxiety has erupted in several countries into public unrest.
Exam-related turmoil has led to mass student protests in Mexico after nearly 60,000 university applicants were forced to resit tests amid suspected cheating, while Portugal’s disastrous attempt to digitise school exam marking sparked the country’s worst education crisis in decades.
By far the largest and most ground-shaking incident was in India, however, where an exam paper leak affected millions of students and was linked to more than a dozen students taking their own lives. The scandal forced the education minister to resign, and challenged the government’s hold over its 1.4 billion citizens.
Why does this exam season seem to be particularly tense and volatile? Experts say the growth of AI cheating and attempts by academic institutions to digitise examinations are at the heart of the issue. When coupled with the high stakes of good grades in an increasingly precarious global economy, the result can be explosive.
“It would seem that exams are getting more fraught on a global scale,” said Dr Sarah Eaton of the Werklund School of Education at the University of Calgary. “The pressure on young people has absolutely changed.
“We’ve seen the economic situation change around the world in the last decade. And the results of one examination determining a person’s entire future really creates untenable pressure on young people,” said Eaton, a leading expert on academic ethics. “This is a tragedy when young people are dying by suicide because of an examination outcome.”
When a single test can determine a young person’s entire future, cheating is no longer just about individuals but becomes a systematic issue, said Eaton. This is compounded when illicit commercial industries, known as the “education mafia”, exploit student desperation by stealing and then selling exam papers, something that has become widespread in India and elsewhere.
Students from across India joined the mass demonstrations led by the Cockroach Janta party, a youth-led protest campaign that began as an online satirical joke and grew into a nationwide outcry that poses an unprecedented challenge to Narendra Modi’s government.
“When you get large-scale fraud combined with systemic failure, there’s almost a guarantee of a breakdown of public trust,” said Eaton. “And once that trust is broken, it’s almost impossible to regain. I can’t imagine how India is going to deal with this, just given the levels of corruption and fraud that we’ve seen.”
In Portugal, the national fallout from a failed push by its education minister, Fernando Alexandre, to fully digitise the exam marking process has landed the government in a crisis. Parents, teachers, and students have been protesting, demanding Alexandre’s resignation after his policy resulted in serious marking errors.
Similar demonstrations took place in Mexico. The National Autonomous University of Mexico (Unam), the country’s most prestigious university, announced that due to abnormally high marks in entrance exam results, which raised suspicions of widespread cheating, approximately 58,000 students would have to retake the exam.
Schools worldwide are rushing to deal with AI use by students, either through bans or teaching AI literacy and ethics to pupils. Denmark announced this month that from the new term, teenagers would have to make a verbal defence of their written essays to combat AI cheating.
Eaton has implemented similar reforms in her class. “AI can generate a perfect essay in seconds. So an essay is no longer a viable way to demonstrate students’ learning,” she said. “We should let it die with dignity and find other ways to assess student learning.”
In Eaton’s view, cheating is a “human problem” and so grading and assessing student learning has historically also been a human responsibility, which she said cannot easily be off-loaded to the latest tech.
But what institutions around the world have been doing instead, she said, is hoping technology can be easily and cheaply used to prevent cheating en masse.
Dr Thomas Lancaster, a computer scientist at Imperial College London who researches the educational use of generative AI, has studied how cheating has gone hi-tech. It is no longer about sneaking notes written on a sleeve, he said, but sophisticated communication.
Lancaster says students have always cheated but it has become far easier, with pupils using earpieces or miniature cameras, and increasingly, communicating with friends or family with access to internet searches.
“I think the number of notes you sneak in, they’re only useful if they’re the right notes and if you can interpret them very quickly,” he said.
“But with any kind of communication technology, you can have that expertise waiting outside for you in a human form. They either know the answers; they’ve got the expertise; or they can look them up online. You can go further than that now and have access to AI to communicate directly during the exam as well,” he added. “It’s spy technology, really.”
Rather than individual student misconduct, Eaton said the failure to properly train educators was forcing students to spend valuable time trying to navigate through these “broken” systems rather than focusing on learning.
“This idea of these mass examinations happening at scale, it sort of dehumanises the learning process and the assessment process,” she said.
This, she said, “sort of perpetuates this idea that examinations are the most important thing for students. I think we’ve lost the thread. Learning should be the most important thing for students.”

The 1991 treaty that still haunts the Kremlin
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-16
07:00:00 UTC
16:00:00 KST

As Russia wages war on Ukraine, denying its own history of aggression against its neighbours, a little-known treaty signed 35 years ago is quietly getting in the way of the Kremlin's narrative.
In July 1991, five months before the Soviet Union formally dissolved, Russia signed a treaty with Lithuania in which it recognised something Moscow has spent the past two decades trying to erase from the record: that the Soviet Union illegally annexed Lithuania in 1940, and that Lithuania's independence, declared in 1990, was legitimate.
That document is still in force. Russia has never torn it up. And that, say Lithuanian officials and legal experts, makes it an awkward loose end for a Kremlin that now insists the Baltic states were never really occupied at all.
Under President Vladimir Putin, Russian state doctrine has increasingly leaned on the claim that the Baltic states joined the USSR voluntarily, and that talk of "occupation" is Western-backed revisionism.
That framing underpins not only Moscow's rhetoric towards Lithuania, Latvia and Estonia but also, in a broader sense, the ideological justification for its invasion of Ukraine – the idea that the borders and independence of post-Soviet states are negotiable, or fictional.
The 1991 treaty directly contradicts that. Dainius Žalimas, a Lithuanian MEP who has studied the treaty closely, argues that its first article, which has no expiry date, remains one of Lithuania's strongest legal cards: it commits both countries to recognising each other as sovereign states with an inalienable right to independence, and bars either from meddling in each other's internal affairs as well as using or threatening force against the other.
"All of this essentially refutes every claim made by current official Russian propaganda, and undermines the very foundations of the ideology of 'rashism'. That ideology, which underpins both the aggression against Ukraine and the denial of Baltic statehood, recognises neither the occupation of Lithuania nor the continuity of the Lithuanian state, among much else," said Žalimas.
"I think the treaty is very important. We talk about the wavering authority of international law, but it gives Lithuania a solid line of international legal defence, and shows that Russia, for very brief periods in its history, can be different," he added.
For example, Lithuania can continue to demand compensation from Russia for the damage caused by occupation, even though few believe this will ever happen in practice.
"Just as the treaty of July 12, 1920 formed the basis for all subsequent treaties with the Soviet Union, the same applies here – dozens of Lithuanian-Russian agreements rest on the July 29, 1991 treaty. So the treaty still holds, as long as they haven't broken it," explained Česlovas Vytautas Stankevičius, former deputy chairman of the Supreme Council and head of the negotiating delegation with Russia, highlighting why the treaty still carries weight to this day.
How it came about
The path to the treaty began in secrecy. In May 1990, Vytautas Landsbergis, then chairman of Lithuania's Supreme Council (the country's parliament in the final Soviet years), held a clandestine meeting with Boris Yeltsin, his Russian counterpart, in an empty Moscow school classroom. The two men barely knew each other personally, and the meeting was arranged through informal contacts.
Two months later, leaders of the three Baltic states and Russia met in the Latvian town of Jūrmala and agreed to pursue bilateral treaties – partly as a way of applying pressure on Mikhail Gorbachev, the Soviet leader, who was still trying to hold the union together.
That effort was not merely symbolic. The USSR spent 1990 and 1991 trying to force Lithuania, as well as other republics, back into line, including a 75-day economic blockade after its declaration of independence.
At the time, it was unclear whether it was better to negotiate with the Soviet leadership or with Russia, which in June 1990 had issued its own declaration of state sovereignty. As a result, negotiations proceeded with both the Soviet authorities and with Yeltsin's Russia, which proved to be a great decision since once the Soviet Union collapsed, Russia became its legal successor.
For Lithuania, negotiating and signing the treaty meant securing the backing of the largest Soviet republic for its independence – a powerful argument against the Soviet Union. Meanwhile, Russia's leadership was competing during with the central Soviet authorities for control.
"The goals of the two states coincided," summarized Stankevičius, who was appointed head of Lithuania's negotiating delegation.
Having concluded treaties with Latvia and Estonia, Russia wanted to sign a similar document with Lithuania.
But Lithuania's treaty took longer to conclude, largely because Vilnius pushed for tougher language than Moscow wanted to accept.
The sticking points
Negotiators clashed over three issues in particular.
The first was citizenship. Lithuania wanted to prevent members of the Soviet military and security apparatus – as well as their families – from automatically qualifying for Lithuanian citizenship, while also avoiding a settlement that would let ethnic Russians resident in the country claim dual nationality.
A compromise formula eventually restricted citizenship rights to those with ties to Russia who had lived and worked in Lithuania since before November 1989.
The second was how to characterise the movement of people under Soviet rule – specifically, how to avoid a formula that would have put Lithuanians deported to Russia by Stalin's regime in the same legal category as Russians who had been resettled into Lithuania as part of Soviet colonisation policy.
The two sides eventually agreed on the neutral term "relocating persons" to cover both groups without equating them politically.
Finally, the thorniest question – whether Russia would accept responsibility for the 1940 annexation – was resolved not by the negotiating teams but by Landsbergis and Yeltsin personally.
"The Russian negotiators didn't want to accept responsibility for crimes committed by the Bolsheviks – all those acts of violence and coercion against neighbouring states. They didn't want the responsibility. Their position was that the Russian Federation, in restoring its own statehood, would not take on responsibility for the crimes of the communist regime," Stankevičius told LRT.lt.
Meanwhile, Landsbergis's own public position at the time was that responsibility lay with the USSR rather than Russia specifically.
So, the compromise text kept a reference to the 1940 annexation while dropping Lithuania's request to invoke an earlier, 1920 peace treaty in which Soviet Russia had renounced all claims to Lithuanian territory, making it's later Soviet occupation – illegal.
The irony
That compromise proved more significant than either side may have anticipated. When the Soviet Union collapsed months later, Russia inherited its rights and obligations as successor state – including, Lithuanian officials argue, responsibility for the consequences of the 1940 annexation that Russia itself had just agreed to acknowledge. And so, it was obliged to remedy the damage, withdraw its troops, and so on.
Three and a half decades on, the treaty's core value lies precisely in the fact that it is Moscow's own signature on a document that says the opposite of what the Kremlin now claims.

Will the rallies continue if it becomes clear that Fedorov will definitely not return to his former ministerial post?
And if they do continue, how long can they last?
For now, this question remains open. All the more so because the main grievance of part of society toward Zelensky is not so much about Fedorov as it is about the systemic problems that forced Zelensky to dismiss the defense minister – even knowing that this would cause dissatisfaction.

How the US could squeeze Iran with economic isolation – and the risks involved

How the US could squeeze Iran with economic isolation – and the risks involved
The Treasury Department is exploring targeting Chinese banks, shadow fleets and exchange houses, but secondary sanctions risk economic blowback
Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent says the US is getting ready to squeeze Iran with unprecedented economic pressure, a claim critics greeted with scepticism given the country is already subject to a naval blockade and thousands of sanctions.
While the Trump administration has not said what it is planning to do, there are still pressure points that Bessent’s Treasury Department could hit. The main challenge is that targeting the remaining options risks blowback on the US economy.
“Unless the president decides to prioritise addressing the Iran threat over all other issues, and namely China, it’s unlikely any action they take is going to materially change Iran’s calculus,” Bloomberg Economics analyst Chris Kennedy said.
Below is a look at a few options. They are far from exhaustive and it remains unclear which, if any, the administration will pursue. Officials could combine several of these measures or opt for a different approach altogether.
China buys more than 90 per cent of Iran’s oil exports. Penalties on entities that facilitate these purchases would directly reduce Tehran’s oil revenues.
Washington has already sanctioned some Chinese teapot refineries and firms since the US started the war against Iran in late February. But so far, the US has stopped short of targeting the major Chinese banks that finance the trade.
The risk is that hitting Chinese companies or financial institutions risks worsening tensions with Beijing ahead of a planned meeting between US President Donald Trump and Chinese leader Xi Jinping. There is also an economic trade-off, since curtailing Iranian barrels would remove discounted crude from the global market and could lift already elevated oil prices.

Troops from North Korea to boost Russia's Ukraine forces
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-16
06:49:00 UTC
15:49:00 KST

Troops from North Korea to boost Russia's Ukraine forces
August 16, 2026
In late 2024, North Korea sent troops to help defend the Kursk region of Russia from Ukraine. International officials estimate that 14,000-15,000 North Korean troops were initially deployed to assist Russia in its war in Ukraine..
Now, Ukrainian and international intelligence agencies suspect that North Korea is planning to send an additional 30,000-50,000 troops to Russia. Ukrainian officials have also stated that North Korean ballistic missiles are being fired from Russia.
President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has raised concerns that North Korea's improved combat and weapons experience could pose a security threat to Ukraine, as well as the Asia-Pacific region.
Defense in Russia
Observers have had mixed responses to Zelenskyy's remarks. Oleksandr Kovalenko, a military and political expert at the Ukrainian Center for Security Studies, told DW that new troops from North Korea would likely be used to secure Russia's border territories. Aside from remaining in Kursk, North Korean soldiers could also help secure southwestern Vornezh.
"These forces could free up Russian occupational forces," Kovalenko said. "Russia would then be able to deploy around 15,000 troops to battles along front lines in Vovchansk, Kharkiv, Sumy or even Chernihiv."
Kovalenko does not expect North Korean troops to fight on Ukrainian territory.
The Russian military analyst Ruslan Leviev agrees. "It's one thing to recapture Russian territory," he told DW, "and an entirely different thing to be present on internationally recognized Ukrainian territory, taking part in a war of aggression."
"Diplomatically speaking," he said, "those are two entirely different concepts."
Russia not outgunned
Leviev said he had not seen concrete evidence of a noteworthy North Korean presence in Russia. He said Moscow had enough troops available without having to draw foreign soldiers into the fight.
"If you look at the front line, you can see that Russia's forces have been fairly active since mid-July," Leviev said. "That's a clear sign they still have enough forces."
Estimates by the economist Janis Kluge, of the German Institute for International and Security Affairs (SWP), back this up. "While Russia's recruitment campaign has shown signs of strain this year, regional spending figures indicate that Russia is still recruiting around 1,000 contract soldiers each day," he recently wrote in a report.
Intelligence on North Korea's short- and medium-range ballistic systems, the KN-23 and KN-24, is far less speculative. Ukraine's Main Directorate of Intelligence (HUR) states that North Korea has delivered 148 KN-23 and KN-24 missiles since 2025.
In July, Zelenskyy said one such missile had struck a home near Ukraine's Kryvyi Rih, killing two parents and three children.
The HUR recently reported that a North Korean missile unit was deploying to Russia's Voronezh region, where it could be equipped with 120 ballistic missiles. Zelenskyy has taken this as indication that Russia's strategic reserve is depleted.
Kovalenko has come to a different conclusion. Instead of having run out of reserves, he said, he believes that Russia is looking to launch a higher number of missiles "to spread more terror."
'Instruments of terror'
Ukrainian military sources say North Korean missiles are similar to Russia's Iskander missiles, but with a greater payload, longer range and lower accuracy.
The military expert Yuri Fyodorov calls North Korea's missiles "instruments of terror." He told DW that "it is very difficult to hit a small target with North Korean weapons." He said he believed that Russia had deliberately targeted residential areas with these missiles.
Like the Russian Iskander 9M723, KN-23 and KN-24 missiles can only be stopped by US-made Patriot air-defense systems, which Ukraine has run critically low on.
Leviev said ballistic missiles would play a key role in this phase of the war. As Ukraine's stockpiles run low, he said, it will become a growing priority to Russia to keep a steady supply.
This summer, Leviev said, he has seen Russia launch far more ballistic missiles than in previous years. Should Russia's missile supply run low by winter, he said, "there will still be North Korea reserves, to make sure Ukraine cannot catch its breath."
No turning point
None of the experts DW spoke with believes that North Korea's involvement will bring about a turning point in Russia's war with Ukraine.
Jenny Town, of the US-based Foreign Policy Research Institute, said the time had passed for North Korea's involvement to make a significant difference. Instead, she said, Russia and North Korea have established a mutually beneficial partnership that is only likely to deepen through the course of the war with Ukraine.
Kovalenko also doesn't expect Russia to make substantial territorial gains along the front lines, but he is concerned about the upcoming winter. "October, November and December could become very trying for Ukraine," he said.
Russian forces could benefit from a possible new military call up, from freeing up fighters it replaces with North Korean troops and from a further stream of ballistic missiles. "That would be no good for the course of the war, and for Ukraine's war interests," Fyodorov said.
This article was originally written in Russian.

Russia has lost around 1,467,320 troops in Ukraine since the beginning of its full-scale invasion on Feb. 24, 2022, the General Staff of the Armed Forces of Ukraine reported on Aug. 16.
The figure includes 1,510 casualties Russian forces suffered over the past day.
According to the report, Russia has also lost 12,270 tanks, 25,151 armored combat vehicles, 134,851 vehicles and fuel tanks, 47,007 artillery systems, 2,034 multiple launch rocket systems, 1,570 air defense systems, 439 aircraft, 354 helicopters, 463,404 unmanned aerial vehicles, 2,257 unmanned ground systems, 35 ships and boats, and two submarines.
Ukraine's General Staff has not revealed its own losses during the full-scale invasion, citing operational secrecy.
Independent Western think-tank reports agree that the Russian casualties significantly surpass Ukraine's losses, with the Center for Strategic and International Studies (CSIS) estimating the ratio to be "roughly 2.5:1 or 2:1."
A January 2026 CSIS report said Ukraine has likely suffered between 500,000 and 600,000 casualties from February 2022 to December 2025, of which between 100,000 to 140,000 are thought to be killed in action (KIA).
While Ukrainian officials rarely disclose the figure, President Volodymyr Zelensky told France TV on Feb. 4 that at least 55,000 Ukrainian soldiers have been killed in action since the beginning of the full-scale war, in addition to a lot more missing in action (MIAs). The intensity of Russian drones and the fighting has made it extremely difficult for Ukraine to retrieve the bodies of fallen soldiers, which are needed for DNA confirmation.

Taichung uses AI cameras, drones to crack down on illegal open burning

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Taichung’s Environmental Protection Bureau said Saturday that its artificial intelligence camera system and aerial drones have detected hundreds of cases of illegal open burning, resulting in NT$1.28 million (US$39,000) in fines, according to a Taichung City Government press release.
The bureau said it began deploying AI smoke-detecting cameras along with drones in 2022. When the camera system detects abnormal air pollution, it alerts authorities, who then deploy drones and send inspectors to the location.
The bureau said the ground-and-air surveillance network has caught hundreds of cases of unauthorized open burning, with fines totaling NT$1.28 million. The bureau added that nearly 170 AI smoke-detection systems have been installed across Taichung to improve enforcement efficiency.
The bureau said open burning harms air quality and may cause fires. Under the Air Pollution Control Act, violators can be fined up to NT$100,000, while industrial or commercial facilities can face fines of up to NT$5 million, the bureau said.

Chinese ship sets off for Europe through Arctic, halving travel time
- A Chinese container ship, Dubai Tower, has begun a new route through the Arctic's Northern Sea Route, cutting travel time to Europe by half.
- The route avoids the Suez Canal and Red Sea, reducing risks from Middle East conflicts but is only open during ice melt seasons.
- Environmental groups warn this increased Arctic shipping may speed ice melt, while China promotes the route as part of its "Polar Silk Road" plan.
AI generated
BEIJING – A Chinese container vessel has set sail for Europe through the Arctic, part of a new weekly service on a route that cuts shipment times in half but which environmental groups warn could speed up the melting of polar ice.
The Dubai Tower left the eastern port city of Ningbo on the evening of Aug 15 heading north, where it will pass through the Bering Strait, then turn west through the frigid waters along Russia’s northern coast. It is expected to reach Felixstowe in Britain on Sept 7, followed by stops in Hamburg, Germany and Gdynia, Poland later that week, according to a timetable published by Sea Legend.
The Northern Sea Route (NSR) from China to Europe is significantly faster than that through the Suez Canal and allows vessels to avoid the Red Sea, where shipping has been targeted by Iran-backed Houthis in Yemen.
But the route is accessible only during the time of the year when the ice is melted enough to allow transits without icebreakers.
Global shipping is heavily disrupted by war in the Middle East, sparked by US-Israeli strikes on Iran in late February.
Other shipping companies have transited the Arctic passage before, with Denmark’s Maersk the first to do so in 2018. In 2025, 23 container ships transited through, up from 15 in 2024, according to shipping analysis from business insurer Allianz Commercial.
Environmental groups warn that increasing numbers of ships transiting the shorter NSR could accelerate loss of Arctic sea ice – already made vulnerable by rising global temperatures.
Major shipping companies including France’s CMA CGM, Switzerland-headquartered MSC and Germany-based Hapag-Lloyd have pledged to “avoid Arctic transshipment routes”.
Analysts say the Arctic could serve as an important future trade route, particularly for China, which has outlined plans for greater access to the region through a “Polar Silk Road”. AFP

Jharkhand students and aspirants protest

Across China: Return of delicate aquatic plant signals Chinese lake's revival
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-16
14:35:11 CST
15:35:11 KST

Workers harvest Ottelia acuminata at a planting base at Yong'an Village of Eryuan County in Dali Bai Autonomous Prefecture, southwest China's Yunnan Province, on Oct. 18, 2024.(Photo by Luo Xincai/Xinhua)
KUNMING, Aug. 16 (Xinhua) -- Under the summer sun, Erhai Lake in southwest China's Yunnan Province glistens thanks to its clear blue water dotted with floating white blossoms. Tourists stroll and cycle around the spot, where limpid waters, lush mountains and blooming flowers combine in weaving a picturesque scene.
The delicate blossom seen floating there is Ottelia acuminata, an aquatic plant endemic to China, which is known to have extremely strict water quality requirements. It demands high water transparency, cleanliness and calcium content, and survives only in unpolluted waters, serving as a reliable natural indicator of aquatic ecological health.
Its large-scale revival vividly testifies to Erhai Lake's remarkable ecological restoration achievements.
China's Ecological and Environmental Code, enacted on Saturday, stipulates nationwide protection and restoration of river and lake ecosystems, providing solid legal support for systematic water ecological governance across the country.
As China advances its Beautiful China initiative, this code is expected to strengthen rule-of-law guarantees for ecological protection and provide fresh impetus for the country's green and low-carbon transition.
In the early 1990s, agricultural pollution worsened Erhai Lake's water quality, causing frequent blue-green algae outbreaks. A severe algae bloom hit the lake in 1996, leaving the water turbid and smelly. As the environment degraded, Ottelia acuminata nearly disappeared from the lake.
Thanks to years of targeted ecological protection and restoration efforts, the lake's water quality has improved steadily, maintaining an excellent Grade II standard from January to June 2026, and creating favorable conditions for the return of Ottelia acuminata.
Official data show that the plant's coverage on Erhai Lake has surged from 90,000 square meters in 2021 to 950,000 square meters in 2026, marking a remarkable ecological recovery.
The improved water environment has also brought tangible economic benefits, turning the lake's ecological advantages into a sustainable industry. From lake ecology to farm cultivation and consumer products, Ottelia acuminata's dual ecological and economic value has been fully realized.
In 2018, environmental worker Zhong Lan noticed the edible plant's great potential for water purification and industrial development. With support from local authorities and Shanghai Jiao Tong University in eastern China, she started a company and built a professional research base in 2024, developing standardized planting techniques that enable high-yield, repeated harvests and offering jobs for local villagers.
Villager Li Xinyuan, who quit Ottelia acuminata cultivation years ago due to low profits, resumed planting in 2023 and earns a stable monthly salary of 4,500 yuan (about 663 U.S. dollars) at the base.
His fellow villager Du Hongquan earned over 100,000 yuan last year from growing the plant and has more than doubled his planting area this year. "The base takes full charge of sales, so we can plant without any worries," Du said.
Eryuan County, the source of Erhai Lake, now has more than 200 hectares of Ottelia acuminata plantation area, creating numerous jobs yearly. The plant has been developed into a diverse range of products like tea, plant-based coffee and cookies.
"I used to think it was exclusive to Yunnan, but I can try it elsewhere too," said a tourist surnamed Ai after tasting the plant at a hotpot restaurant in Hangzhou, east China's Zhejiang Province.
The beautiful lakeside scenery at Erhai has also boosted local tourism. In 2025, Dali received over 120 million tourist visits, attracting visitors to enjoy lake views and experience local Bai ethnic culture, with 407,000 long-term visitors.
Last month, the State Council issued a plan for building a Beautiful China during the 15th Five-Year Plan period (2026-2030), setting out the overall requirements, targets, key tasks and major projects for comprehensively advancing this initiative.
According to the plan, China will achieve overall improvement in ecological and environmental quality and make significant progress toward building a Beautiful China by 2030, with green production and lifestyles largely established and the carbon peaking target reached on schedule. ■

BEIJING, Aug. 16 (Xinhua) -- China's Ministry of Emergency Management has sent 13 emergency drainage teams to the city of Zhoukou in central China's Henan Province to assist with urban waterlogging relief efforts, the ministry said on Sunday.

Taiwan groups warn of Taiwan Strait security risks due to Japan's neo-militarism
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-16
14:34:52 CST
15:34:52 KST

TAIPEI, Aug. 16 (Xinhua) -- Several Taiwan-based groups have voiced opposition to Japan's neo-militarism, warning that Tokyo's push for a greater military role in regional affairs could undermine peace and stability across the Taiwan Strait and throughout East Asia.
Their concerns were expressed at forums, seminars and a public gathering held on Friday and Saturday, as Aug. 15 this year marks the 81st anniversary of Japan's unconditional surrender in World War II.
At a forum in Taipei, more than 10 organizations, including the Reunification Alliance Party, brought together scholars and experts from both sides of the Taiwan Strait, as well as from Hong Kong Special Administrative Region, Japan and Australia.
Participants called on people on both sides of the Strait and across Asia to draw lessons from history, oppose the expansionist ambitions of Japanese right-wing forces, and safeguard peace and stability in East Asia.
Citing remarks previously made by Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi, Wang Yung, president of the Reunification Alliance Party and host of the forum, said they suggested the possibility of Japan's military intervention in Taiwan-related affairs and represented a key sign of the country's accelerating remilitarization.
The Japanese government was seeking to loosen the constraints imposed by its pacifist Constitution and the long-standing post-war principle of an "exclusively defense-oriented policy," Wang noted, warning that such moves could have serious repercussions for security in the Taiwan Strait and peace in East Asia.
A seminar was also held on Saturday in Taichung, central Taiwan, drawing over 30 descendants of resistance fighters who fought against Japanese aggression, as well as historians, teachers and students.
The event was jointly organized by several Taiwan-based groups, including an association representing relatives of patriots who fought against Japanese aggression.
Li Su-hui, daughter of anti-Japanese resistance fighter Li Tsang-chiang, said her family retained painful memories of resistance to Japanese colonial rule in Taiwan from 1895 to 1945.
"Remembering history is not merely about paying tribute to those who came before us, but also about passing on the spirit of resistance from generation to generation," Li said.
She voiced concern over the resurgence of Japanese right-wing forces and signs of militarism re-emerging, saying the seminar could help young people develop a proper understanding of their national identity and history.
"We are part of the Chinese nation, and the lessons of history must not be forgotten," Li said.
Shaw Kai-ping, also a descendant of an anti-Japanese resistance fighter, warned of the risks posed by both a revival of Japanese militarism and growing secessionist activities in Taiwan.
"At a time when the Democratic Progressive Party authorities are vigorously promoting a secessionist narrative, we need to stand up and help more people in Taiwan recognize that our motherland is China and our ancestral homeland is on the Chinese mainland," he said.
On Friday, several civic groups, such as the Reunification Alliance Party and the Labor Party, gathered and protested outside the Japan-Taiwan Exchange Association in Taipei.
Wu Jung-yuan, chairman of the Labor Party, said Japan's war of aggression against China had caused more than 35 million Chinese casualties, while Taiwan endured 50 years of Japanese colonial rule, inflicting profound suffering on people on both sides of the Taiwan Strait.
"Taiwan is part of China," Wu said, calling on people on both sides of the Strait to work together to oppose external interference, safeguard peace and stability across the Strait, and strive for national reunification. ■

JOHANNESBURG, Aug. 16 (Xinhua) -- Growing agricultural cooperation with China is opening up new opportunities for South Africa's farming sector, giving fresh impetus to production and rural economic development, an industry representative has said.
In an interview with Xinhua, Andre van der Vyver, executive director of the South African Cereals and Oilseeds Trade Association, called enhancing cooperation with China "very important."
"It is a reliable market that we can depend on over the medium to long term," he said.
Under the cooperation, exports would encourage production and add more value to the local economy, specifically the regional and rural economies, he said.
China, a major soybean importer, offers South African producers access to a large and diversified market, van der Vyver said, adding that such access would provide the scale and certainty needed to support the continued expansion of South Africa's agricultural sector.
Applauding China's zero-tariff treatment for qualifying South African products, he said that, combined with South Africa's geographical freight advantage over major competitors, the removal of the tariff provides an important boost to exporters.
The tariff arrangement could also create opportunities for a wider range of agricultural products, including maize and fruit, van der Vyver added.
Beyond commodities, he said, there was considerable scope to deepen cooperation across the agricultural value chain, including agricultural equipment, technology, logistics, infrastructure and market access.
Van der Vyver said that South Africa has already imported Chinese agricultural equipment, and that Chinese expertise and investment in infrastructure could help address major constraints facing the country's agricultural exporters, particularly in rail, roads and ports.
"The interaction of exporting products while leveraging China's technology, equipment, and infrastructure capabilities creates a very valuable bilateral trade relationship moving forward," he said.
"Partnering with China will definitely add strong value to our agricultural sector and rural economies, so we are very excited about it," said van der Vyver. ■

'Not where the problems are': Working holiday visa slowdown divides parties
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-16
06:31:04 UTC
15:31:04 KST

In Brief:
- The government is slowing down processing of working holiday visa applications.
- The Nationals and One Nation say backpackers aren't the problem, instead placing blame on international student numbers.
The federal government has confirmed it will slow the processing of working holiday visa applications as pressure mounts to reduce net migration numbers.
Nine newspapers first reported on Saturday that the federal government had paused applications for working holiday visas from 24 countries.
But Home Affairs Minister Tony Burke confirmed on Sunday that working holiday visas were still being processed, but they were being handled "more slowly than they were previously".
He did not provide further information about the reason for the slowdown.
However, when asked about the impact of fewer backpackers on the agriculture sector, he pointed to a Pacific workers' scheme as the primary visa for temporary staff.
News that makes sense
Your trusted source for staying up-to-date with the world around you. Get free daily news updates and analysis, straight to your inbox.
"One of the things that happened when we started to improve worker protections on (the Pacific scheme) was ... some of the worst operators said, "if we've got to have better standards for (those) workers, we'll just switch to backpackers".
"That's not the way this system's meant to work."
SBS has contacted the Home Affairs department for comment.
Working holiday visas — often called "backpacker visas" — allow travellers to extend their stay in Australia by undertaking work that addresses labour shortages in Australia — often fruit picking, farm work, mining, or tourism work in regional and remote areas.
Migration in the spotlight again
The number of working holiday visa holders in Australia passed 210,000 in June 2025, outpacing pre-COVID figures by around 100,000.
The move comes as pressure builds on the Albanese government to bring down net overseas migration, with other parties carving out their migration policy.
Migration experts have warned of the dangers of political parties attempting to blame migrants for a lack of homes, arguing that migrant workforces will be essential to building the required housing stock
Net overseas migration — a measure covering visitors, family and partner visas, working holidaymakers, skilled migration, and humanitarian intake, alongside returning Australians — fell slightly to 301,000 in 2025, down from 306,000 the year before, according to the Australian Bureau of Statistics.
Labor's long-term target is 225,000 a year over the next three years, though Burke said on Sunday the party's migration policy was still being worked through and needed to go through a full cabinet process.
None of the major parties has yet specified which visa categories they'd cut to hit their targets — though the Coalition has said intake should be tied to housing competitions rather than a fixed annual figure.
Coalition frontbencher Andrew Bragg raised eyebrows last week when he floated cutting net overseas migration to 180,000 a year, suggesting the figure could be reached through "modest reductions" to international students, working holidaymakers and post-study work visas — a mix he said would bring housing supply back in line with population growth.
The Coalition itself is yet to land on an annual migration target or a formal policy for reducing the intake.
Nationals reject changes for backpackers
But the Nationals and One Nation have historically backed working holiday visas for the role they play supporting regional and remote areas, and both parties' leaders spoke out against the government's move on Sunday.
"The system we've got with working holiday visas has worked — and worked for a long time," Nationals leader Matt Canavan said on Sunday.
"It's not where the problems are."
Canavan said there was still a problem with "too many" people coming into Australia and settling in metropolitan areas, which he said was driving "massive housing stress" and pressures on infrastructure — but said backpackers weren't part of that.
"It's not backpackers that are taking away houses from people in Sydney and Melbourne or Brisbane," Canavan said, instead pointing to what he called an "unprecedented surge in student visas" as the real problem, backing a cap on international student numbers at 25 per cent of the current intake.
"We don't think our universities should be skewed and biased towards trying to find an income stream to teach overseas students — they should be skewed and biased towards teaching Australians and doing Australian research," he said.
"That's the system that has to change and where we should put our focus on."
One Nation leader Pauline Hanson, who wants net migration cut to 130,000 a year, agreed the reduction should come from international students, calling the university intake system a "scam" that she claimed provided a backdoor to Australia.
But she was firm that any cuts should leave backpacker numbers alone.
"We cannot stop those people coming in; if they did, the farmers would go under," Hanson said on Sunday.
'One Nation has gone too far': Nationals
On Saturday, Hanson also called for the government to immediately block migration — including refugee and humanitarian visas — from countries on the Department of Foreign Affairs' "do not travel" list, arguing they pose a security risk.
Canavan distanced himself from that proposal on Sunday, saying he was "very concerned" by it.
"One Nation has just gone too far," he said.
"The very reason that many of these countries are on the 'do not travel' list is because they are host to some of the most tyrannical and oppressive regimes in the world … it is in these parts of the world where most of the persecuted Christians and other minorities live."
"I think the question to One Nation here is: if you go this far, aren't we just losing something of what it means to be Australian, that we are welcoming people … and we do welcome people who want to be in this country that contribute to it and ultimately become fantastic Australians?"
Labor MP Chris Bowen dismissed Hanson's idea on Saturday and compared it to something United States President Donald Trump would enact.
"Australia needs an Australian immigration policy, not one stolen from Donald Trump," he said.
"Some of the countries on that list have provided Australia with wonderful migrants ... Iraq, Lebanon, countries like Afghanistan.
"People who have fled ISIS, who have come to Australia for refuge and knowing they've received refuge, have started small businesses, contributed to our community".
— With additional reporting by Australian Associated Press.

Thousands of evacuees await aid after deadly quake on Indonesia's Flores island
